Wholesale and Retail Sector

The Adaptation Plan for the Wholesale and Retail sector is designed to support the development
and implementation of an effective sectoral adaptation strategy and action plan to form part of
Antigua and Barbuda’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP), ultimately designed to reduce
vulnerability and enhance the resilience of the Wholesale and Retail sector. The key objectives of
this project were to conduct a situational analysis of the sector to include a review of key
documents and policies; lead consultations with key stakeholders to map climate risks to the
sector; to assess the vulnerability of the sector based on national, regional, and global trends in
climate and current and projected economic variables; to identify entry points within institutional,
policy, and legislative frameworks for prioritized adaptation actions; and to develop a Monitoring,
Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) plan that outlines an approach to integrating adaptation options
in sectoral policies and plans with related indicators for monitoring and evaluation. The outcomes
of these tasks informed the creation of this adaptation plan. The plan is intended to support the
DOE to prioritize adaptation actions that reduce vulnerability and enhance resilience of the sector.




                                                                                                       CHAPTER 3: IMPLEMENTING ADAPTATION
Although the primary user for this plan is the DOE, the W&R sector have a role in leading some of
the implementation actions.

Background
Generally, the wholesale and retail sector are defined as a two-distribution arrangement that
constitutes a major part of the supply chain, meaning that when goods are manufactured, they
are sold in large quantities (wholesale) to the wholesalers who further sells them to the retailers
who finally sells them to the ultimate customers. The wholesale and retail sector therefore
represents the critical link between manufacture and consumption. The wholesale and retail
sector includes 136 establishments with a little over 90 per cent of these establishments being in
retail with a little less than 10 per cent of the total being wholesale establishments.

Of the 136 establishments, two operated both in wholesale and retail – one of these
establishments is in the Dairy Product, Beverage Product and Manufacturing Industry and the
other is in the Grocery Stores Industry. The sector is dominated by the grocery stores industry and
the hardware, plumbing, building materials and supplies industry. The wholesale and retail trade
sector contributed to approximately 12% of the GDP in 2021

The economy of Antigua and Barbuda is predominantly a service economy. According to the
Labour Force Survey Report, two out of every three workers (66.9%) in Antigua and Barbuda
worked in services industries in 2018. The hotel and restaurants industry were the largest
employer with 17.4 percent of the employed population. Public administration and defence were
the second largest, followed by wholesale and retail trade with 11.0 percent (Antigua and Barbuda
Ministry of Finance and Corporate Governance, Statistics Division, 2020). It is important to
recognize that these sectors do not stand alone but work together to create the overall economy.
The Wholesale and Retail sector is vital to this system. As importers and sellers of necessary goods
in the country, negative impacts it experiences will ripple through the other sectors as well.




                                                                                                 94
                                            An^gua and Barbuda Na^onal Adapta^on Plan


Approximately 5,517 people are employed in the wholesale and retail sector, representing about
16 percent of the employed force (UN Women). The sector employs the second largest number
of workers, with the first being the hotels and restaurants sector which employs 17 percent of the
labour force. In 2018, the number of men and women employed in the wholesale and retail sector
was almost equal. In addition, wholesale and retail was one of the top two industries that female
managers worked in (Antigua and Barbuda Ministry of Finance and Corporate Governance,
Statistics Division, 2015).

Implementation

The adaptive technologies and strategies are designed to reduce vulnerability and enhance
resilience of the wholesale and retail sector to climate change. Four key adaptation action areas
were identified which are:
            ○ Physical adaptation and policy planning
            ○ Climate proofing wholesale and retail buildings




                                                                                                           CHAPTER 3: IMPLEMENTING ADAPTATION
            ○ Financing and financial instruments for adaptation
            ○ Training, capacity building, knowledge transfer for adaptation, and business
                continuity planning

The first area, physical adaptation, and policy planning is focused on the built environment and
improving its resilience and reducing its vulnerability. The goal of this area is to ensure that climate
change impacts are considered when planning and designing infrastructure, deciding locations,
and construction principles. They include structural and engineering options to harden
infrastructure as well as urban planning instruments such as land-use planning and the
development, application, and enforcement of building codes. The wholesale and retail sectoral
adaptation plan lays out specific projects that would work towards building resilience, reducing
vulnerabilities, and incorporating adaptive strategies in the building sector.

The second area, climate proofing wholesale and retail buildings, focuses on adaptation actions
to climate-proof buildings pertaining to the wholesale and retail sector. Actions are proposed to
make buildings resilient to climate change effects such as heatwaves, coastal flooding, and
hurricane wind and surge.

The third category, financing and financial instruments for adaptation, considers finance and
economic instruments for adaptation activities and disaster recovery from public, private,
alternative, or blended sources. Access to finance and insurance cover is a major concern for
Antigua and Barbuda businesses. There are several approaches being used currently in adaptation
planning and implementation in different parts of the world. The government could offer financing
instruments including loans, bonds, and seed capital. Insurance (micro, parametric) can be a cost-
effective tool for adaptation planning and implementation. Several cases exist for insurance
schemes in low income and developing countries which are a partnership project between private
and public entities.

                                           An^gua and Barbuda Na^onal Adapta^on Plan


The fourth category, training, capacity building and knowledge transfer for climate adaptation and
business continuity planning, highlights adaptation actions that strengthen the knowledge and
capacity of the wholesale and retail sector to respond to and adapt to the effects of climate
change. Such measures include knowledge transfer and training on how wholesale and retail
businesses can structure their strategic plans to consider and include climate change adaptation
practices and design effective business continuity plans that factor in climate change effects.

Local Area Adaptation Plans (LAAP)

The Local Area Adaptation Plans (LAAP) that have been developed for three areas in Antigua set a
strategic framework for guiding and integrating the efforts of national and local government, local
development corporations, civil society, businesses, and the international community in
strengthening these areas’ capacities to adapt to climate change between 2023 and 2033. The
three areas that have been considered are the Airport/Fitches Creek Local Area, St John's City, and
the Jolly Harbour to Johnson's Point. These LAAPs provide sets of implementable actions identified




                                                                                                        CHAPTER 3: IMPLEMENTING ADAPTATION
by multiple stakeholders as being key to reducing experienced and projected climate impacts in
the most vulnerable portions of these areas. They also present combinations of cross-sectoral
interventions to strengthen the capacity of the institutions that will play key roles in planning the
adaptation actions and integrating these adaptation considerations into current and future
development agendas, plans, programmes, and projects. These LAAPs serve as living documents
that should undergo periodic revision and modification, where needed. The adaptation options
and strategies included in these LAAPs identify indicative lead institutions. The period for
implementing the measures, within the LAAP 2023-2033 cycle will be contingent on the availability
of both the financial and technical resources required to implement and execute the actions
outlined.

LAAP Function and Audience
The LAAPs have been formulated to:
   1. Inform the process of planning, coordinating, and implementing actions urgently needed
      throughout the three local areas defined to prepare for, and cope with, the impacts of
      climate variability and change in the medium and long term and, when possible, tap into
      opportunities to address climate change.
   2. Guide the integration of climate change adaptation considerations into ongoing, planned
      and emerging decision-making processes developed for the portions within each of the
      three areas that are deemed most vulnerable to climate impacts by stakeholders, i.e.,
      critical infrastructure and facilities, the built environment and residential communities,
      natural ecosystems, tourism and local businesses.
   3. Raise awareness on climate change projections, vulnerabilities, challenges and proposed
      solutions to promote action for the three defined areas, and encourage collaboration
      between, ministries, departments, parliamentary representatives and inter-ministerial
      committees to support the integration of climate change adaptation considerations in all



                                                                                                  96
                                          An^gua and Barbuda Na^onal Adapta^on Plan


      decisions made on ongoing and new development activities, programmes, projects and
      investments for these areas between 2023 and 2033.
   4. Be an instrument for the mobilization of resources. The priority measures recommended
      can be included in projects to be presented to, and funded by, regional and/or
      international climate finance sources and can also be used by long-standing donor agencies
      to identify activities to support, based on their own funding priorities and preferences. It
      is also expected that, where possible, national resources will be allocated to adaptation as
      these considerations are increasingly included into national development policies, plans
      and programmes.

Goal and Objectives
The following adaptation goal and objectives help to provide a structure for the next steps, by
clearly defining what the local area stakeholders would like to achieve through adaptation actions.
The success of this LAAP will be reliant on the degree to which the overarching goal is

accomplished to yield actual climate impact risk reductions.

To increase the technical and physical capacity of St. John's City, the Jolly Harbour to Johnson's
Point local area, and Airport/Fitches Creek local area to prepare for the impacts of climate change
as they seek to become climate-robust areas through effective and coordinated adaptation
efforts.

Guiding Principles and Cross-cutting Themes
The LAAPs are aligned in particular with the National Communications (NCs) to the UNFCCC, and
the guides and plans recently developed to advance the overall NAP process. As such, the
development of these plans retained some of the same fundamental principles and cross-cutting
themes of this NAP which includes:
   ➢ Ownership: LAAP should be integrated into sectoral policies and plans so that the entire
       government and key local stakeholders commit to and take ownership of climate-resilient
       development.
   ➢ Considerations on demography, gender and social inclusion: the LAAPs and the
     recommended actions will take into account the differentiated impacts of climate change

St John’s City Local Area Adaptation Plan

St. John’s City is the capital of Antigua and Barbuda which is located on the northwest coast of
Antigua, adjacent to a sheltered natural deep-water harbour. The demarcated area of focus is
bordered by St. John’s Harbour to the west; Dickenson Bay Street to the north; Stapleton Lane,
Independence Avenue and Camacho Avenue to the east; and the Grays Farm Main Road to the
south. Surrounding St. John’s City is St. John’s Rural which makes up the remainder of the St. John’s
parish. St. John's City is the most urban and developed area in the country and serves as the chief
commercial centre and port of entry for Antigua. It is also the largest city in the country, being
approximately 10 km2 in size, with a maximum elevation of 59 meters (194 feet) above mean sea
level.

One of the main hazards that threaten livelihoods in the St John’s City local area is flooding,
particularly flash flooding following heavy rains. Stakeholders consulted have indicated that
flooding is more prominent in areas near the coast, along watercourses, and major drain systems
for areas further inland (Figure 3-3). This is linked to the topography of St. John’s City, as eastern
sections are elevated and gently slope westward to St. John’s Harbour, ending in a coastal plain
that is flat and low-lying. As a result, areas along the coastline are prone to flooding from heavy
prolonged rainfall events. In the past, flood waters triggered by such events have resulted in
surface water levels high enough to restrict access to roadways and sidewalks, damage low-lying
building structures, flood homes, stores, stalls, and businesses, limit vehicular traffic flow and
disrupt the activities of both local and tourist-based pedestrians and shoppers.

The low-lying coastal nature of St. John’s City also puts coastal infrastructure and operations at

coastal structures will be more susceptible to flooding.

demand, however, is a challenge, since rainfall has decreased in the Caribbean in the last century
(as established under the Mainstreaming Adaptation to Climate Change (MACC) Project, 2010)
with below-average rainfall being recorded across the Caribbean in 2015 (NOAA, 2015).

Process for Sourcing Funding

In the pursuit of funding for NAP implementation for Antigua and Barbuda, a systematic approach
is essential to navigate the climate finance landscape. This section outlines a structured process
for sourcing funding, beginning with the critical task of problem prioritization. By identifying and
ranking environmental issues based on urgency and impact, stakeholders can lay the foundation
for targeted interventions. The subsequent phases delve into the project idea conceptualization,

Problem Prioritization

Sustainable Island Resource Framework (SIRF) Fund

The GoAB has established the Sustainable Island Resource Framework Fund (SIRF Fund) as the
central conduit for receiving environmental, climate mitigation, and adaptation financing from
both international and domestic sources. The SIRF Fund was created as a Special Fund in
accordance with the Finance Administration Act (2006).

The SIRF Fund has the responsibility of facilitating funding access for the public sector, private
sector, as well as non-governmental and community organizations within Antigua and Barbuda.
Additionally, it has the capacity to assist in environmental management efforts across various

islands within the Organization of Eastern Caribbean States (OECS). Income to the SIRF Fund is
derived from a combination of domestic and international channels. Domestically, this includes
revenue generated from Green Card Park visitation fees, pollution charges, carbon credits, taxes,
levies, and any other fees specified by regulations. On the international front, the SIRF Fund
functions as an executing body and a sustainable financing mechanism for bilateral and
multilateral funding sources allocated for the objectives outlined in the Environmental Protection
and Management Act (2019).

The SIRF Fund continues to represent an opportunity for the Government and people of Antigua
and Barbuda to attract substantial financing to support green growth, the Nationally Determined
Contributions (NDCs) targets and an overall sustainable development agenda for the country.

Debt for Climate Swaps

Despite achieving high per capita income and robust growth rates in 2019, Antigua and Barbuda's
economy still maintains a relatively modest scale, marked by persistently elevated levels of public
debt. While recent economic growth, diligent efforts at debt restructuring, and fiscal reforms have
yielded some success in lessening the weight of public debt, the country faces significant
challenges in servicing these debts. This challenge primarily arises from the escalating financial
and economic toll of climate change, which has placed substantial constraints on the nation's fiscal
capacity.

To break free from this challenging financial situation, the GoAB has initiated discussions with both
the GCF and their creditors who are part of the Paris Club. The objective is to establish a trilateral
arrangement known as a Debt for Climate Swap. In this innovative arrangement, the GCF would
provide financial support or partial financing to facilitate the repurposing of Antigua and Barbuda's

domestic initiatives focused on climate change projects within the country.

enhance its institutional and technical capabilities for securing and leveraging climate finance. A

Insurance prospective for farmers and fishers

The likelihood of agricultural losses in Antigua and Barbuda is on the rise because of climate
change, particularly concerning factors like droughts and strong winds. While farmers and fishers
are implementing specific measures to mitigate these risks, there is a pressing need to improve
and formalize the entire risk management system. A comprehensive approach to risk




                                                                                                      CHAPTER 4: FINANCING STRATEGY
management should address the vulnerability of farmers and fishers to climate change impacts in
Antigua and Barbuda.

A study was conducted by the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) in collaboration with
the Department of Environment (DOE) to report on the Insurance prospective for farmers and
fishers in Antigua and Barbuda. One of the major findings in this study was that the agricultural
insurance that would cover the production losses of farmers and fishers is not present yet in the
country but is highly needed as a risk transfer instrument in the face of climate change.

Subsequently, recommendations made by the UNDP included that Insurance companies join their
efforts with the government in financial education of fishers and farmers: explaining which
insurance products are already available and in which cases they bring the benefits.

Additionally, two possible insurance types were suggested for Antigua and Barbuda – indemnity
insurance and/or parametric insurance. Indemnity insurance can provide the coverage for all risk
categories (climatic and man-made), whereas parametric insurance would only cover measurable
climatic risks.

All in all, further assessments along with these recommendations will help in insurance product
development moving forward for the agricultural sector as well as other sectors that are highly
impacted by climate change.

Private Sector Engagement Strategy for NDC

Antigua and Barbuda’s Private Sector Engagement Strategy establishes a systematic approach for
the public sector to collaborate with private sector entities to align action and mobilise resources
to achieve the country’s NDC targets and commitments. The strategy focuses on supporting
country efforts to reduce emissions to support the NDC implementation, while facilitating a clean
energy and sustainable transition. Private sector engagement is a key element to achieving the
country’s NDC due to the private sector’s contribution by adopting greener policies and practices
and undertaking the transformation towards a more sustainable and circular supply chain. The
strategy lays out a four-phased approach to ensure meaningful and effective collaboration and
progress.

Phase 1 establishes the initiation of engagement to lay a foundation for long-lasting collaboration
through the entire implementation process. This is followed by Phase 2 on providing stakeholders
with necessary information to make informed decisions. Phase 3 involves the formalization of
engagement and decision-making of collaboration mechanisms into institutional structures.
Finally, Phase 4 establishes an iterative process to the strategy to reflect feedback, reflections,

5. Overview of Monitoring & Evaluation
The NAP’s Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning (MEL) Framework takes into consideration the
individual adaptation actions prioritized through the NAP preparation process and is based on the
NAP technical guidelines:31
    1. Monitoring of adapta^on ac^ons in An^gua and Barbuda,
    2. Reviewing the NAP process to assess progress, eﬀec^veness, and gaps,
    3. Itera^vely upda^ng the na^onal adapta^on plan,
    4. Promo^ng outreach on the NAP process, and




                                                                                                                                 CHAPTER 5: MONITORING, EVALUATION AND LEARNING FOR ADAPTATION
    5. Repor^ng on progress and eﬀec^veness

The MEL Framework incorporates the process of collecting, analysing, and using data for the
purpose of measuring whether adaptation actions are being implemented according to plan
(monitoring). Monitoring of adaptation is an ongoing process of collecting data and documenting
information to determine progress made against stated plans. Monitoring should reveal whether
activities lead to the achievement of outputs and planned targets. Monitoring is, therefore, useful
for identifying issues during implementation to provide feedback needed by decision-makers. It
looks at measurable changes linked to inputs, processes, and outputs. The processes of review,
assessment, and learning is key to monitoring.

The Framework links the monitoring process with that of evaluation. Evaluation of adaptation
should further assess the management and impact of adaptation actions to determine if they are
having the desired results. The Framework promotes reporting of findings to multiple
stakeholders. To uphold the principles of transparency and accountability, it promotes the sharing
of lessons, knowledge, and best practices (learning) for continuous improvement of adaptation
efforts. Learning will be generated from implementation experiences and inform decision-making,
ongoing adaptation, and future planning efforts.

Monitoring and evaluation are distinguished mainly in terms of their purpose, the time periods
when they are done, why they are done, what they measure and who is involved. Monitoring is
conducted continuously to gather information on implementation status at a given time, or over
time. It involves identifying data needs, collecting, and analysing data, and using that data in
relation to activities, processes, outputs, and progress towards meeting outcomes. Based on the
information gathered, the results are used for decision-making, to solve implementation problems
and to make corrective changes.

Contrastingly, the focus of evaluation is on assessing design of policies, strategies, plans and
interventions; as well as the implementation process, outputs, outcomes, and impacts achieved.
At its core, evaluation provides insight on what works well, what has not worked, what needs to
change, and gives structured insight into the overall performance. Evaluation provides needed
evidence to allow for corrective actions to be taken when needed. Both processes, however, do
allow for the modification of existing plans based on lessons learned.

Institutional Arrangements

The DOE is primarily responsible for coordinating the implementation of the National Adaptation
Plan. The DOE is an accredited National Implementing Entity to the Adaptation Fund (AF) and a
direct access Accredited Entity (AE) to the Global Environment Facility (GEF), and therefore is in a
position to coordinate the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) in
the country as well as climate finance. These agreements pertain to inter alia climate change,
biodiversity, and land degradation. Antigua and Barbuda’s context as a small island developing
state (SIDS) necessitates streamlining of its institutional structures. The government, therefore,
aims to strategically build capacity for MEAs in one agency (i.e., the DoE) to provide enhanced
accountability and coordination across all agencies and stakeholders.

In accordance with its mandate, the DOE coordinates multistakeholder technical and oversight
committees. A key coordination committee is the country’s Technical Advisory Committee (TAC).
The TAC currently consists of over 15 members from Government, as well as NGO and private
sector representatives. The Project Management Committee (PMC) is a high-level oversight

There is a connection between effective adaptation and ongoing reflection and
learning. Promoting feedback and learning on adaptation involves analysing M&E data to learn
from implementation experiences and informing decision-making, ongoing adaptation, and
planning for future initiatives. Learning is a critical and continuous process that occurs throughout
this cycle of planning, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, all of which contribute to
knowledge creation. An effective M&E system of adaptation facilitates learning and
accountability, which are essential elements of results-based management.

Antigua and Barbuda will provide dedicated resources to transfer knowledge and lessons learned
on national adaptation planning. To do so the country will:
   • Synthesize experiences, best prac^ces and lessons learned and incorporate these into
       Na^onal Communica^ons, the Adapta^on Communica^ons and policies, plans, strategies
       and key reports.
   • promote the use of the sub-regional OECS climate resilient Building Code and include
       ﬁndings from the NAP process in the updated Building Code.
   • Provide outcomes of na^onal adapta^on planning to the Finance Sector (banks and
       insurance) in the sub-region and via the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB) to allow
       them to make climate resilient ﬁnancial decisions and where appropriate, provide detailed
       risk informa^on to the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF); and
   • Share knowledge, lessons learned and best prac^ces at the Conference of Par^es, regional

5.12. Conclusion

As the climate crisis escalates, the Government of Antigua and Barbuda has been bearing the costs
of adaptation – recovering from hurricanes, making improvements to infrastructure, adapting to
saltwater intrusion, installing desalination and water storage, among other actions. This effort is
not unique to Antigua and Barbuda. Climate expenses and recovery activities borne by the
Government tend to delay the implementation of developmental priorities. In addition to the
Government, the private sector and other stakeholder groups have also had to invest in
adaptation planning.

This makes tracking national adaptation planning progress even more crucial. An integral part of

mainstreaming into national development processes. Importantly, it will also synthesize data and
information generated making it accessible to a variety of stakeholders – from government

                               FOREWORD
      Viet Nam is one of the nations severely affected by global climate change, which represents
a huge challenge for the country’s sustainable development. To join the global efforts to respond
to climate change, Viet Nam signed and ratified the Paris Agreement in 2016 and updated its
Nationally Determined Contributions in 2020 and 2022 which include the contribution to
climate change adaptation.
     Climate change adaptation has also been legalised in the Law on Environmental Protection
2020, providing a legal foundation for Viet Nam to develop, promulgate and implement the
National Strategy on Climate Change to 2050, the National Adaptation Plan for the period 2021
- 2030, with a vision to 2050, and the National Climate Change Adaptation Monitoring and
Evaluation System.
      In implementing the responsibilities of a signatory to the Paris Agreement and the provisions
of the Law on Environmental Protection 2020, the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment
of Viet Nam has led and coordinated with line ministries, sectors, experts and international
partners to prepare the Report on the National Adaptation Plan for the period 2021 - 2030, with
a vision to 2050 (updated). This report provides complete and comprehensive information about
climate change trends in the past and at present, and projected climate change information in the
future; analyses the impacts of climate change, including risk factors, vulnerabilities of sectors,
branches, regions and different groups in the society; evaluates the results achieved by the
country’s efforts; identifies and clarifies shortcomings, thereby proposes objectives, tasks and
solutions to enhance resilience and adaptability to adverse impacts induced by climate change,
reduce vulnerability and risks, losses and damages; and promotes the integration of climate
change adaptation into the national, sectoral, and local development strategies and plans.
     The Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment highly appreciates the active
participation of various ministries, sectors, and provinces, as well as research agencies,
socio-political organisations; and development partners, experts and scientists; the support
of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the United Nations Entity for Gender
Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN Women); and the enthusiastic and responsible
contributions and inputs of organisations and individuals in the preparation of the Report.
     We hope to continue to receive cooperation from other countries and development
partners to effectively implement the National Adaptation Plan in the future.

    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


         1. THE RATIONALE OF THE NATIONAL ADAPTATION PLAN
         Viet Nam is a country that is vulnerable to the impacts of climate change (CC). Viet Nam has
    a coastline of approximately 3,260 km and a sea area of  approximately 1 million km2, including
    the Paracel and Spratly archipelagos, with over 3,000 large and small islands along the coast.
    The area of Viet Nam’s mainland territory is about 331,230.8 km2, with three quarters being hills
    and mountains; the rest are alluvial plains, of which two large deltas are densely populated and
    particularly vulnerable to climate change, especially to sea level rise.
         In Viet Nam, climate change has negatively impacted all sectors, fields, and provinces,
    posing a real threat to the country’s sustainable development and poverty reduction goals,
    requiring timely actions to mitigate damages and strengthen climate risk management and
    disaster prevention. The development and implementation of the National Adaptation Plan
    helps to effectively use resources, enhance capacity in financial and technical management
    and coordination, avoid overlaps and duplications, and promote the engagement of
    communities, businesses, and international organisations in fulfilling the national adaptation
    objectives. Therefore, the development and implementation of the National Adaptation Plan
    (NAP) is necessary.
         Viet Nam developed the National Adaptation Plan for the period 2021 - 2030, with a vision
    to 2050 as per the Decision No. 1055/QD-TTg of the Prime Minister dated July 20, 2020. After
    a period of implementation, given the new context, Viet Nam further updated the National
    Adaptation Plan for the period 2021 - 2030, with a vision to 2050, which was issued by the
    Prime Minister on November 19, 2024. The implementation of the National Adaptation Plan
    aims to reduce vulnerability and risks to the negative impacts of climate change by enhancing
    the resilience and adaptation capacity of the country’s natural and socio-economic systems,
    thereby minimising losses and damages caused by climate change.
         The updated National Adaptation Plan builds on the provisions on climate change
    response stipulated in the Law on Environmental Protection (LEP) and prevailling policies on

      Chapter I. Introduction: Presents an overall introduction to Viet Nam’s national context,
legal grounds, methodology, process for the development of the NAP, and report layout.
      Chapter II. Climate change in Viet Nam: Presents historical and current climate change
trends, based on monitoring data and future climate change scenarios; the increase in climate
risks; the impacts of climate change on different sectors, regions, and vulnerable groups in Viet
Nam; and current and future climate change-induced losses and damages for Viet Nam.
     Chapter III. Achievements and gaps in climate change adaptation: Assesses and analyses
the achievements in policies, actions, and mobilisation of financial resources for climate
change adaptation, as well as gaps in climate change adaptation at the national, sectoral,
and provincial levels, covering different aspects including institutions, policies, finance,
science, and technology; the integration of climate change adaptation (CCA) into development
plans; coordination among ministries and sectors; regional linkages; social engagement; and
international cooperation.
     Chapter IV. National Adaptation Plan: Presents objectives, tasks, and some specific targets
to achieve, along with tasks and priority solutions to adapt to climate change in the period 2021
- 2030 that have been specifically identified for different sectors, fields, and regions based on
the analysed achievements, gaps, and vulnerabilities, as well as the coordination mechanisms
among ministries, sectors, provinces, and organisations for implementing these solutions; NAP
organisation of implementation; NAP monitoring and evaluation; NAP implementation phases;
and financial resources for NAP implementation.
      Chapter V. Challenges and need for international support: Analyses difficulties and

adaptation capacity.
     3. OBJECTIVES AND SCOPE
     - Overall objective: Mitigate vulnerability and risks from the negative impacts of CC by
strengthening the resilience and adaptation capacity of natural, economic, and social systems;
minimise losses and damages caused by CC; and promote the integration of CCA into strategies
and plans.
     - Specific objectives: i) Enhance the resilience and adaptation capacity of natural, economic,
and social systems and ensure sustainable livelihoods; enhance capacity and awareness to
be ready to adjust to climate change; ii) Mitigate natural disaster risks and minimise damage
caused by increasing natural disasters and climate extremes, contributing to addressing CC-
induced losses and damages; and iii) Improve institutions, promote potential and resources for
effective CCA, and promote the integration of CCA into strategies and plans.

           4. TASKS AND SOLUTIONS
           (1). Enhance the resilience and adaptation capacity of natural, economic, and social
      systems and ensure sustainable livelihoods
           Enhance the resilience and adaptation capacity of natural, economic, and social systems
      and ensure sustainable livelihoods by investing in CCA actions to effectively use and prevent
      the depletion and degradation of resources; developing CCA and climate-smart agriculture;
      protecting and developing forests and ecosystems; developing infrastructure systems;
      strengthening medical and healthcare systems; and ensuring social security and gender equality.
           a) Effectively use and prevent the depletion and degradation of resources
            - Implement national water resources planning, establish and implement integrated
      river basin plans which identify areas that require strict protection. Investigate and evaluate
      underground water sources, effectively and flexibly manage underground water extraction in
      areas affected by climate change and saltwater intrusion, and prevent degradation, depletion,
      and pollution of water sources.
            - Promote the search, exploration, and extraction of water sources to ensure water supply
      for the domestic use and production of people in mountainous areas, ethnic minority areas,
      border and island areas, areas with difficult and extremely difficult socio-economic conditions,
      and areas with freshwater scarcity.
           - Encourage organisations and individuals to invest in researching and applying advanced
      science and technology to manage, protect, and sustainably develop water resources, extract
      and use water resources efficiently and effectively, collect and use rainwater, artificially
      supplement underground water, restore polluted, degraded, and depleted water sources, and
      prevent and overcome the consequences of water shortage.
           - Monitor, supervise, and evaluate transboundary water resources and strengthen
      international cooperation to protect and prevent the depletion and degradation of transboundary
      water resources.
           - Rationally and effectively use idle land areas, alluvial land along rivers and coasts for
      forest development, and green tree development in urban areas and industrial zones. Strengthen
      solutions to improve and protect the soil environment, especially for degraded agricultural land;
      prevent and minimise soil degradation due to erosion, drought, and saltwater intrusion.
           - Strictly manage mineral resources used as common construction materials, ensure the
      prevention of landslides, subsidence, and sea encroachment.
           b) Develop climate-resilient and climate-smart agriculture
           - Implement climate-resilient and smart agriculture; improve the efficiency of
      agricultural land use, rationally arrange crop structure, convert part of the rice area to high-
      value, economically efficient crops or rice–aquaculture areas; make use of and promote the
      advantages of tropical agriculture.
          - Develop organic, ecological, low-GHG emission, and environmentally friendly agriculture
      based on the natural advantages of each region and market demand.
           - Promote regional cooperation and linkages, develop agricultural product value chains
      or key raw material zones; plan production areas and the development of large-scale, modern,
      concentrated commercial agriculture.

     c) Manage, protect, and develop forests and ecosystems
     - Strictly protect existing natural forests; enhance the protective capacity of watershed
forests and coastal forests; restore and develop coastal mangroves, develop large timber
forests, and restore forest landscapes; manage forest resources sustainably in association
with biodiversity protection and the enhancement of natural ecosystem services; promote
community engagement in forest protection, management, and development; consolidate and
complete the system of monitoring and evaluation and emergency response to forest fires.
    - Manage ecosystems; strengthen the resilience of natural ecosystems; and protect and
conserve biodiversity against CC impacts and sea level rise.
     - Establish, expand, and improve the quality of nature reserves, with a focus on marine
protected areas; develop nature-based, ecosystem-based, and community-based models for
CCA; conduct inventory, assessment, and development of the national database on biodiversity.
     d) Develop CCA infrastructure
     - Make plans; invest in developing the infrastructure of industrial parks, urban and residential
areas, and resettlement areas based on disaster risk zoning and CC scenarios. Upgrade and
renovate sectoral infrastructure and simultaneously implement measures on environmental
protection and CCA.
      - Develop CC-resilient urban areas, urban infrastructure, concentrated residential areas,
industrial parks, and resettlement areas along the coast and islands; develop urban areas, coastal
cities, sea tourism, and eco-tourism hubs; promote the development of synchronous, modern,
interconnected CC-resilient housing, and urban infrastructure systems; and apply sustainable
cooling solutions and new CC-resilient materials in the construction and urban sectors.
     - Build, upgrade, and renovate medical facilities and schools to ensure their resilience
to CC impacts and natural disasters; strengthen adaptation capacity in the event of natural
disasters and evacuation in case of natural disaster emergencies.
      - Upgrade and renovate traffic works in areas with a high risk of natural disasters and
vulnerability to climate change; develop and perfect the expressway network and inter-regional
traffic connection system.
      - Build and upgrade drainage systems and prevent flooding due to heavy rains, floods, high
tides, and storm surges for large urban areas and coastal urban areas. Focus on completing
freshwater storage works for daily needs and production; build and complete the system of
irrigation works; build a number of new large multi-purpose reservoirs in drought and water-
scarce areas.
     - Strengthen capacity and infrastructure to provide clean water to residents, paying
attention to rural, mountainous, and coastal areas, especially those affected by storms, floods,
droughts, and saltwater intrusion.
     e) Strengthen medical and healthcare systems
      - Develop a network of medical and healthcare systems to meet requirements for the
prevention and control of new CC-induced epidemics and diseases which prioritises vulnerable
groups and ethnic minority areas. Build and replicate models of healthcare and public health
in order to improve community resilience and CC adaptability. Strengthen communication and
CCA capacity of health sector.
     - Develop a system of monitoring and early warning of CC impacts on health.

           (2). Mitigate natural disaster risks and minimise damage caused by increasing natural
      disasters and climate extremes, contributing to addressing CC-induced losses and damages
           Implement solutions to enhance capacity for forecasting and early warning of natural
      disasters, extreme weather, and climate conditions; improve the climate risk assessment and

      surveillance systems serving the prevention and control of storms, tropical depressions, heavy
      rains, floods, flash floods, inundation, landslides, droughts, and saltwater intrusion. Socialise
      part of the extreme climate monitoring and supervision, with priority given to the socialisation of
      automatic rain gauge systems.
           - Apply advanced and modern forecasting technologies; prioritise the development of
      technologies for quantitative rain forecasts, flash flood and landslide warnings, multi-disaster
      warnings, and impact-based forecasts; deploy diverse hydrometeorological forecast and
      warning products transmitted on digital technology platforms; build capacity in providing
      climate services and information to serve the natural disaster prevention and control.
           - Strengthen disaster information transmission capacity in combination with the national
      information and communication infrastructure system to ensure complete, accurate,
      and timely transmission and distribution of information to serve effective natural disaster
      prevention and control.
           - Investigate and assess the level of climate change impacts on urban areas; delimit
      areas at risk of being vastly affected by climate change; calculate the capacity and level of self-
      adaptation and propose response solutions.
           - Improve the disaster risk management system, complete the assessment and zoning of
      climate and disaster risks, and create disaster warning maps; build and complete the national

      sea dyke systems; build and upgrade storm shelters for ships and boats according to plans and
      linked to logistics services and fisheries information, including island areas.
           - Build and consolidate works to prevent and control riverbank and coastal erosion in
      areas with complex erosion, seriously threatening dyke systems, residential areas, and
      important infrastructure.

INTRODUCTION

     1.1. COUNTRY CONTEXT
      Viet Nam is located in Southeast Asia, bordering China to the north, Laos PDR and Cambodia
to the west, and the East Sea to the east and south. It has a coastline of approximately 3,260 km
and a sea area of  approximately 1 million km2, including the Paracel archipelago (in Da Nang
City) and the Spratly archipelago (in Khanh Hoa province), along with more than 3,000 large
and small islands along the coast. The area of Viet Nam’s mainland territory is approximately
331,230.8 km2, with three quarters being hills and mountains; the rest are alluvial plains, of
which the Mekong River Delta and the Red River Delta are the most densely populated in the
whole country and particularly vulnerable to climate change, especially to sea level rise.
     Viet Nam’s population in 2023 was 100.3 million people, of which the urban population
was 38.2 million (38.1%), the rural population was 62.1 million (61.9%), and the average life
expectancy was 73.7 years. In terms of economic structure, as of 2021 the agriculture, forestry,
and fishery sectors accounted for 11.96%; the industry and construction sectors accounted
for 37.12%; the service sector accounted for 42.54%; product taxes after deducting product
subsidies accounted for 8.38%; and GDP per capita was 4,284 USD.
     Viet Nam experiences a tropical and monsoon climate, with an average temperature of
about 28oC. Average rainfall in areas mostly ranges from 1,400 mm to 2,400 mm per annum.
Viet Nam often suffers from storms, tropical depressions, floods, inundation, strong tides,
and droughts. In recent years, due to CC impacts, extreme weather events have been tending
to increase in both quantity and intensity, severely affecting the stability and sustainable
development of the country.

         1.2.2. Steps for NAP development
          The NAP was drafted based on the guiding documents from the UNFCCC and the regulations
    of Viet Nam. Drafting steps include:
          - Step 1. Collect information and data: Information on the current status and trends in CC,
    data serving the study, an assessment on the impacts and vulnerability, and an assessment of
    Viet Nam’s current needs for CCA were reviewed and gathered from such sources as climate
    change and sea level rise scenarios, action plans on CC response from ministries, sectors,
    and provinces, the results of scientific studies on CC by national and international research
    institutes and universities, activities related to CCA, and annual reports from ministries, sectors
    and provinces submitted to MONRE, especially monitoring information and data of MONRE in
    different periods. MONRE also conducted field survey trips to assess the current status as well
    as CC response work nationwide.
         - Step 2. Analyse and assess CC impacts and identify challenges and gaps in CCA, based
    upon which, propose tasks and solutions to adapt to CC: Research, analysis, and assessments
    on CC impacts and vulnerability to CC of different sectors, fields, and provinces, based on data
    on the current CC situation, Viet Nam’s updated 2020 CC scenarios, sectoral development
    plans, provincial socio-economic development plans, etc. The findings of the analysis and
    assessments have identified sectors and fields that are more affected by and vulnerable to CC,
    as well as the need for prioritised adaptation activities, including agriculture, natural disaster
    prevention and control (NDPC), environment and biodiversity, water resources, infrastructure
    (transport, construction and urban, industry, energy), and others (public health, labour-society,
    culture-sports-tourism). The desk review of relevant documents also showed frequent barriers
    to CCA implementation, i.e., limitations in human resources, technology, budget allocations for
    adaptation activities given the complicated developments of CC in Viet Nam.
         The results of the analysis and assessments were used as a basis to determine the tasks
    and priority solutions for the CCA activities of ministries, sectors, and provinces. The CCA tasks
    and solutions for each field were synthesised and proposed in the NAP in order to achieve the
    overall objective set out and to implement during different phases to 2030, with a vision to 2050.
         - Step 3. Develop the NAP: Viet Nam’s CCA tasks and solutions were proposed to be
    implemented in order to achieve the objectives set out in the NAP. CCA activities were proposed
    by sectors and fields. Regarding the sequence: in the first stage of implementation, activities

     2.3. CLIMATE CHANGE IMPACTS ON VIET NAM
     2.3.1. Increasing CC-induced risks
     Viet Nam is one of the countries heavily affected by CC. Increased exposure of people and
property to hazards is the main driver of the increase in long-term economic losses from weather
and climate-related disasters.
     The extent of CC vulnerability varies from region to region. The Central Coastal areas and the
Mekong Delta are highly exposed to CC impacts but moderately vulnerable to climate change.
Though exposure is not high in the Northern mountainous area, its poverty rate is, making its
vulnerability high as well.
      With a coastline of 3,260 km and islands and seas, Viet Nam will be among the countries
that suffer the most from the risks and potential impacts related to CC and sea level rise. Risks
are increasingly higher in deltas and large urban areas, especially in coastal cities with high
population density, where urban/spatial planning is not taking CC into account, and where there
is a high concentration of assets, infrastructure, and populations prone to damage.
     The Northern and Central mountainous regions are at higher risk of flash floods and
landslides. Meanwhile, the Central Coast and South-Central Coast, the Northern Delta,
the Midlands and the Central Highlands are at higher risk and more vulnerable to drought,
water scarcity, and increasing desertification. The Mekong Delta is also facing the impacts of
 20    Report on the National Adaptation Plan for the period 2021 - 2030, with a vision to 2050 (updated)



     inundation due to sea level rise and land subsidence due to geological subsidence, reduced
     alluvium carried to the delta, and over-extraction of groundwater. Ho Chi Minh City and the
     Mekong Delta region have some areas (Ca Mau peninsula including Ca Mau, Bac Lieu and part
     of Can Tho) with a subsidence rate of over 1 cm/year according to monitoring data since 2005.
          The poor, ethnic minorities, people with climate-dependent incomes, the elderly, women,
     children, and sick people are the most vulnerable to CC. Ethnic minority women are especially
     highly vulnerable to the adverse impacts of CC due to their limited access to education and
     opportunities to engage in non-farm work.
          The fields facing the highest CC-induced risks are agriculture, food security, biodiversity,
     water resources, public health, housing, and technical infrastructure. These sectors and fields are
     highly exposed and sensitive to natural disasters and extreme climate events. CC is an existential
     threat to the goal of hunger eradication, poverty reduction, and sustainable development.
          According to MONRE’s research results, an increase in extreme weather events leads to
     increased risks to vulnerable regions, sectors, and groups. In the future, due to CC impacts and
     sea level rise, the potential flooding could lead to the loss of agricultural land, while water for
     agriculture, domestic, and industrial purposes would be affected by saline intrusion, seriously
     affecting the lives of local population.
          2.3.2. Impacts on different sectors
          2.3.2.1. Impacts on natural resources
          a) Impacts on water resources
           Water resources are most directly and strongly affected by CC, leading to problems
     related to people’s livelihoods, the economy, and the environment. In recent years, the flows in
     major river basins have been lower than the average of many previous years. Dry season flows
     have decreased, water levels in many places have reached historic lows, droughts and water
     shortages have occurred more frequently, and saltwater has intruded further inland.
           According to CC scenarios, compared to the period 1986 - 2005, the annual flows on the
     Red River-Thai Binh River, Ma River, Ca River, Thu Bon River, Ba River, and Mekong River (to Kratie)
     systems have been tending to increase by about 4 - 132%. The flows during the flood season will
     increase by 5 - 178%. The flows during the dry season have been tending to increase by about
     5 - 191%. Of particular note, the flows during the dry season on the Red River - Thai Binh River
     during the period 2016 - 2035 are tending to decrease slightly (by about 0.05%) according to the
     medium scenario.
          Droughts may be more frequent and severe in the Central region. Saline intrusion will be
     especially severe in the Mekong Delta. CC increases and worsens flooding. The highest annual
     flood peak may increase continuously in most river basins, except for some areas such as the
     lower basin of the Red River - Thai Binh River and the Ba River due to the regulation of reservoirs
     and dams. Flash floods and landslides may also occur more frequently and more severely in the
     mountainous areas of the North and Central Highlands.
          CC may lead to a reduction in the absolute elevation of groundwater levels, a reduction in
     the groundwater storage amount, and an increase in the area of salinated groundwater.

is decreasing (World Bank, 2019a). CC and extreme weather events that occur frequently
and irregularly will significantly affect forest resources, causing forest vegetation and forest
ecosystems to change both in area and distribution of forest types. In 2023, the forest area lost

0.89oC and a rainfall increase of 2.5%, the area of this type of forest would be severely reduced,
with the total remaining area estimated to be only about 1.3 million ha (about 3.89% of the total

and are heavily influenced by such factors as climate and hydrology (water flow, salinity, etc.).

with sea level rise, narrow down the area of mangrove ecosystems. The area of mangroves is
shrinking because some plant species cannot adapt to changes in environmental conditions,
such as tidal floods, salinity, and temperature, in a timely manner. Mangrove forest ecosystems
are specifically sensitive to CC impacts. Storms with strong intensity and increased frequency
also destroy mangrove forests. Sea level rise worsens the saline intrusion in estuaries and

     of phytoplankton, etc., which changes the environment in a direction that is unfavourable for the
     growth of seagrass beds. CC also increases ocean acidification and strong storms and destroys
     coral reefs and grasslands, leading to changes in fish species and resources. The mass coral

     2.3.2.2. Impacts on biodiversity
      Mangrove and melaleuca forest ecosystems: These may shrink in area due to the impact
of changes to hydrological regimes, oceanography, waves, and rising sea levels. The area
of mangrove forests is shrinking because some tree species cannot adapt to changes in
environmental conditions, such as tidal flooding, salinity, and temperature. Strong storms also
destroy mangrove forests. Sea level rise will increase the salinisation process in estuaries and
coastal areas, which is the biggest threat to the melaleuca forest ecosystem. Water and soil
salinity exceeding the allowable limit will kill melaleuca forests or shrink their area. If the sea
level rises by 100 cm, about 300 km2 (about 15.8% of the total mangrove forest area of Viet Nam)
will be affected.
     The marine ecosystem in Viet Nam is being heavily affected by CC, and especially the
coastal wetlands, typified by the mangrove areas in Ca Mau, Ho Chi Minh City, Vung Tau and
Nam Dinh. Increased sea water temperatures change the growing season, increase the outbreak
of phytoplankton, etc., which changes the environment in a direction that is unfavourable for
the growth of seagrass beds. CC also increases ocean acidification and strong storms and
destroys coral reefs and grasslands, leading to changes in fish species and resources. The
mass coral deaths seen over the past 20 years were due to a number of reasons, one of which
was the increased sea temperature. Viet Nam’s islands and archipelagos have been directly
and most severely affected by CC and sea level rise, which have been causing inundation. CC
also affects biological resources, changing the ecosystems of mangroves, seagrasses, and
corals on islands nationwide.
      Biodiversity: Viet Nam is one of the 16 countries with the highest levels of biodiversity in
the world  and is also ranked second in East Asia in terms of the number of threatened species.
The national forest area in 2022, including planted forests with open canopy, is 14,790,075
ha, in which, the area of natural forests is 10,134,082 ha, that of planted forests is 4,655,993
ha; and the forest area meeting the criteria for calculating the coverage ratio is 13,926,043 ha.
The national forest coverage ratio is 42.02%. Most of the beautiful birds and large mammals
are gone. There has been a measurable reduction in not only the natural area, but also the
habitat quality of many forests. Out of a total of 310 identified major mammal species, 78 are
threatened (based on the level of national threat), of which 46 are internationally recognised.
CC can change the structure and distribution of biological species and the level of biodiversity
in Viet Nam’s ecosystems. Increased temperatures will result in changes to distribution areas
and biome structure, causing the dispersion of aquatic and marine resources. Sea level rise and
increased storm intensity will result in changes in the composition of sediments, salinity, water
pollution, degradation of, and threats to mangrove forests and their species.

     2.3.2.5. Impacts on urban and housing development
     Climate change is a major threat to urban infrastructure and quality of life. In the context
of CC, urban areas are predicted to be more affected due to the increase in intensity, frequency,
and severity of natural disasters.
      Coastal cities are vulnerable to natural disasters related to storms, floods, and sea level
rise, which increase risks to urban assets, livelihoods, and infrastructure. Urban areas, industrial
zones, coastal economic zones, and urban areas in the Mekong Delta will be the regions mainly
affected by sea level rise. The area from the North to the South-Central Coast is affected by
tropical depressions and storms, but coastal cities are more seriously affected by storms than
other urban areas. Midland and mountainous cities in the North and Central regions are often
affected by post-storm circulation which causes floods, flash floods, and landslides.
      In urban areas, the solid waste treatment system and the urban water supply and drainage
system are the most affected. Increased rainfall will cause flooding in storage points, collection
routes, transportation, and transition, disrupting the solid waste treatment process. CC also
affects water supply sources (surface water, groundwater) and water supply systems, including
key infrastructure and water supply networks.
     Water supply systems in urban areas in the Mekong Delta and the Southern key economic
region are affected moderately to greatly, depending on their location and distance to the sea.
In addition, CC impacts on urban areas (such as droughts and floods) also affect urban water
supply systems, the adaptation capacity of which is mostly medium to low.
      CC and urban development are closely related, and often interact negatively. Rapid
urban development has a strong impact on the nature and increased frequency and severity
of natural disasters. The strong development of urban areas, energy use, and the construction
of infrastructure and high-density buildings all turn cities into energy consumers and generate
many pollutants. When the ground is gradually “concretised,” the space is occupied, and the
water permeability of urban areas in the event of heavy rain will decrease. The loss of land from
water collection to construction also puts existing urban areas and newly planned areas into an
increased likelihood of flooding due to heavy rains.

     2.3.2.7. Impacts on public health
      Many studies around the world show that CC has been adding and will continue to add to
the burden of disease and increase the risk of premature death. One of the main reasons is that
humans are being directly exposed to CC impacts, especially changes in temperature, rainfall,
sea level rise, and greater frequency and intensity of extreme weather events. Human health
is also indirectly affected by CC, such as changes in water reserves and quality, air quality,
food hygiene, and other changes in ecosystems. CC also affects the technical infrastructure
and health system, affecting the capacity of the health system in providing healthcare services,
especially in the event of natural disasters such as droughts, floods, storms, etc.
      a) Impacts on health due to increasing extreme climate events, including heat waves and
severe and damaging cold spells. For heat waves, people face heat stress from working under
high temperatures and humidity, sunstroke, cramps, fainting, heat exhaustion, and even heat
stroke, which, if not treated promptly, could lead to death. According to statistics, when the mean
temperature increases by 1.0oC, the hospitalisation rate increases by 3.4% among children aged
0 - 2, and by 4.6% among children aged 3 - 5. Studies showed that the rate of hospitalisation in
children under 5 due to respiratory infections increased by 3.8% when the mean temperature
increased by 1.0oC.
      Severe and damaging cold spells have many negative effects on human health, especially
for the elderly and people with low resistance. In some areas of Viet Nam in recent years, the
minimum temperature has dropped to -4oC, and long-lasting cold spells have been recorded.
Extreme cold spells can cause acute risks such as cold hands and feet, hypothermia, or an
increased risk of chronic respiratory and other illnesses. In particular, the severe and damaging
cold spells have clear negative impacts on the health of the elderly, children, the poor, those in
poor economic conditions, etc.
     In addition to the negative impacts of extreme temperatures, natural disasters, such as
storms, floods, droughts, and saline intrusion, also affect human health. In recent years, the
increase in strong typhoons has affected human health, leading to deaths, injuries, and mental
health-related problems. In Viet Nam, Typhoon Yagi in September 2024 caused huge damages
and losses to human and properties.
      b) Impacts on human health due to changes in environmental conditions relating to CC
impacts: environmental changes due to CC, such as drought, flooding, sea level rise, etc.,
cause water scarcity, salinisation of agricultural land, pests and diseases, loss of crops and
livelihoods, etc., leading to food shortages or food supply disruptions. Lack of food or disrupted
food supply results in malnutrition and insufficient micronutrient intake among pregnant
women, children, etc.
      Temperature increase presents favourable conditions for many species of organisms, such
as flies, cockroaches, and food-borne vectors to develop. In addition, disease transmission
periods could become year-round. An increase in temperature is often associated with an
increase in the risk of food poisoning and gastrointestinal diseases caused by salmonella.
     Changes in the rain regime lead to drought and a lack of domestic water, putting local
populations at risk of diseases related to contaminated water or water shortages, such as renal
calculi (kidney stones), dermatitis, red eye, etc., as well as gastrointestinal diseases. Inundation
causes skin and digestive diseases.
    Adverse weather patterns often increase the formation of certain air pollutants, affecting
human health.

          2.3.2.8. Impacts on industries
           Industries, especially processing and manufacturing industries, will be affected by CC
     since raw materials for industry, especially the food processing, textile, and garment industries,
     will be significantly reduced due to the lack of supply from raw material zones in provinces and
     regions at risk of disasters and severe inundation and flooding. This will put pressure on the
     restructuring of industries in terms of industry type, proportion of processing industry and high
     tech industry.
          Irregular rains, storms, and sea level rise will negatively affect the operation and use of
     the system of electricity transmission and distribution, drilling rigs, oil and gas pipelines to the
     mainland, and oil supply to oil tankers; increase the cost of maintenance and repair of energy
     works; and affect the supply and consumption of energy and national energy security. For the ore
     mining and processing industry, especially in coastal areas, sea level rise poses the risk of ore
     saline intrusion, affecting ore quality and the production and business activities of enterprises.
           According to a study by the Viet Nam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI), CC
     has negative impacts on the production and business activities of enterprises. Increased
     weather extremes and natural disasters will disrupt production and business, reduce labour
     productivity and revenue, disrupt transportation channels, increase production costs,
     stagnate distribution networks, reduce product quality and cause damages to facilities and
     human resources, etc. Enterprises in the Central Coast and Mekong Delta are being affected
     by disaster risks and CC more than other regions. However, CC not only creates challenges, but
     also offers opportunities for restructuring production, creating new products and technologies,
     and building brands for businesses.
          2.3.2.9. Impacts on energy
          a) Impacts on energy demand
          CC has had strong impacts on energy consumption and demand and has directly affected
     the production of electricity from coal, oil, gas, hydroelectricity, and wind energy. CC not only
     further increases the level of energy dependence, especially for imported energy sources,
     leading to supply instability, but also has a great impact on the safety and stability of the energy
     supply. It also disrupts, stagnates, or even paralyses the energy supply.
           Increased air temperature leads to increased energy consumption, for example in the
     use of more cooling devices, especially during heat waves. According to a report by the Asian
     Development Bank, electricity demand in the period 2005 - 2014 increased by an average
     annual rate of 12.1%, and the demand in the period 2023 - 2028 remains high at 8.5% (Ministry
     of Industry and Trade, 2023). The increase in electricity demand is also due to other reasons,
     such as population growth and socio-economic growth. Increased extraction of groundwater
     and surface water and desalination to meet water demand all increase energy consumption.

     Regarding the power system, when the air temperature increases, the load of the power
system increases, making the power plants, lines, and power stations operate at a higher
intensity. With the power transmission system, when the ambient temperature increases, it will
affect the transmission capacity of the line. For coal, oil, gas and biomass power plants, when
the air temperature increases, the water temperature increases, leading to an increase in the
circulating water for cooling the condenser, decreasing the turbine efficiency, and resulting in
the waste of fuel.
     b) Impacts on energy production and supply capacity
     According to CC scenarios, the number of weak and moderate storms shows a decrease,
while the number of strong to very strong storms shows an increase. The offshore energy and
marine shipping industries are at risk of being impacted by CC as extreme weather becomes
more common. A new IPCC report ‘Oceanography climate change: the impact of climate change
trends on the ocean’ says that the offshore energy sector – particularly assets like oil rigs and wind
power plants – is likely at a higher risk due to worsening extreme weather conditions, including
changes in storm patterns. Offshore facilities may not be designed to withstand climate and
environmental challenges. Inclement weather and tropical storms not only cause unforeseen
damage, but also limit access to sites after incidents, impede maintenance and repair, increase
costs, and cause difficulties for skilled workers, especially in areas that have not previously been
susceptible to such disruptions (IPCC, 2019).
     The coal and mineral industries usually have most of their production, business, and mining
areas located in high mountains, coastal areas, and plains, but a number of raw materials and
production areas are distributed in areas with high terrain (mountain slopes and mountains)
which are easily affected by landslides and flash floods due to heavy and prolonged rains in many
days. Studies show that these impacts, once increased by CC, also contribute to the devastation
of mineral deposits, making it difficult to investigate, evaluate, explore, and exploit minerals,
greatly affecting the process of mine closure and post-mining environmental rehabilitation.
     CC, which causes increased rainfall and floods in the rainy season, adds further difficulties
to production, mining activities, and transportation at mineral mines, leading to human and
property losses for businesses. Many historic heavy rains have affected most of the coal and
mining industry units in Quang Ninh, causing great damage to production and businesses. Many
coal mines were flooded with rainwater, such as Mong Duong, Quang Hanh, Nam Mau, and Hon
Gai, and most of the truck and railway routes transporting coal to ports and specialised roads
suffered landslides, damage, etc. Many factories and mining infrastructure works were filled
with mud.
     CC affects the electricity production process. Changes in rainfall affect the hydrological
regime and river flows, leading to changes in the planning and generation output of hydropower
plants. Abnormal rainfall and flows also affect the ability of hydroelectric plants to supply and
regulate electricity production plans, causing damage to the electricity supply infrastructure,
increasing the cost of new investment, renovation, repair, equipment upgrades, and the
electricity distribution network. In contrast, drought results in reduced power generation time
and power generation efficiency.
      Sea level rise can have impacts on power plants, transmission stations, substations,
fuel pipeline systems, mines, coal yards, and other energy facilities in coastal areas. Sea level
rise and changes in wind speed and clouds, as well as extreme weather events, can affect the
output of wind and solar power projects. Saline intrusion can corrode materials used in energy
production and distribution. In the future, CC is expected to significantly increase risks to energy.

          2.3.2.10. Impacts on trade
          CC and extreme weather events can affect industrial, commercial zones, and infrastructure
     such as roads, electricity, and water supplies for businesses and trading. Heat waves affect
     workers, reducing productivity and affecting commerce. Some commercial and logistics centres
     located in low-lying areas with harbours and other infrastructure are at risk of flooding due to
     sea level rise. Commercial centres, logistics, and infrastructure in the highlands often face the
     potential risk of flash floods and landslides.
          The impacts of extreme heat waves, extreme rainfall, storms, floods, landslides,
     flash floods, and droughts disrupt business operations, reduce labour productivity, disrupt
     transportation and stagnate distribution systems, reduce quality of products and services, and
     damage facilities. They will also cause a shortage of workers, a lack of inputs, and increased
     costs (VCCI & TAF, 2020).
          CC affects export fields such as industry and agriculture. Industrial and commercial areas
     are vulnerable to sea level rise, floods, and storms. Crops are mainly grown in lowland coastal
     areas and plains, which are at risk of sea level rise and saline intrusion. Increasing temperatures,
     variable rainfall, and extreme weather events including storms, floods, and droughts can affect
     all major crops, including rice, coffee, and fruit trees. This will be exacerbated by damages to
     trade-related logistics and transport infrastructure (World Bank, 2022).
           Viet Nam’s trade-related policies need to mention sufficiently CC’s impacts on the trade
     sector. Trade policies can reduce CC impacts by reducing tariffs to improve access to agricultural
     digital services and technologies to increase the productivity and resilience of plants (World
     Bank, 2022).
           According to a modelling study on CC impacts on Viet Nam’s international trade status,
     Viet Nam’s relative competitiveness compared to some countries will be improved but will lose
     its competitiveness against several competitors (AFD, 2021. Chapter 13 in: Espagne E. (ed.)).
          2.3.3. Impacts on different regions
          2.3.3.1. Impact on the deltas
           a) Mekong Delta: The Mekong Delta is considered one of the three large deltas in the world
     most vulnerable to the sea level rise. Climate factors have caused measurable change. In the
     period 1958 - 2014, the annual mean temperature increased by 0.67oC. According to the high
     CC scenario, the temperature by the end of this century will increase by about 3.4oC, with the
     number of hot days increasing by 40 - 60 days; rainfall in the rainy season will increase, but in
     the dry season it will decrease, and the sea level may rise as much as 100 cm, which is likely to
     pose the threat of inundation in up to 47.3% of the delta area. If the sea level rises by 100 cm,
     some 10% of the population in the Mekong Delta will be directly affected due to land loss, and
     the rice growing area will shrink significantly. The areas heavily affected by sea level rise include,
     for example, Tran Van Thoi (Ca Mau), Hong Dan (Bac Lieu), Nga Nam (Soc Trang), Long My (Hau
     Giang), and Giao Thanh (Kien Giang). Saltwater penetrating into estuaries and causing saline
     intrusion, together with droughts, has seriously affected the supply of fresh water and reduced
     the quality of surface and underground water.
          Resolution No. 120/NQ-CP of the Government on the Sustainable and Climate-Resilient
     Development of the Mekong Delta in Viet Nam was issued in 2017 and has gained important
     achievements, including the initial completion of the system of mechanisms and policies to
     promote the development of modern and sustainable agriculture; the development of urban
