2.8.2 Economic Appraisal for the NAP Process

Nigeria’s NAP integrated the findings of a rigorous cost-benefit analysis (CBA)
of Nigeria’s priority adaptation strategies, conducted within the framework of its
National Adaptation Plan (NAP) Process. The CBA aims to guide strategic decision-
making by policymakers, development partners, and stakeholders involved in
climate adaptation planning, identifying cost-effective, high-impact strategies
that can enhance community resilience, stimulate economic growth, and promote
sustainable development in Nigeria.

The CBA analysis focused on the agriculture, water resources, and energy sectors,
identified as highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change (Annex 2). The
analysis adopted the same two Representative Concentration Pathways, RCP 4.5
(aligned with SSP2-4.5) and RCP 8.5 (aligned with SSP5-8.5), used in the Climate
Risk Assessment (FMEnv-EA, 2025); used 2024 as the reference year for valuation;


                                                     National Adaptation Plan (NAP)            27
 set the exchange rate at ₦1,472.1475/US$ (the average exchange rate of 2024);
and applied a 10% social discount rate with an 8% sensitivity. It also used 3-4%
per annum GDP growth; a 12% long-term average inflation rate; and population
projections of 223 million in 2024, projected to reach 263 million by 2035 and over
300 million by 2050 as baseline economic parameters.

The CBA considered 5 adaptation strategies across the agriculture, water resources,
and energy sectors, identified through the CRA impact-chain process, sectoral
policy reviews, and stakeholder consultations, as shown in Table 2.2. Following
identification of adaptation options, a structured cost estimation process was
undertaken, using upfront costs (CAPEX), operating costs (O&M), and expected
economic, social, and environmental benefits over a 35-year horizon. The cost-
benefit analysis (CBA) applied two core profitability indicators - the Net Present
Value (NPV) and the Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) - to assess the economic viability of
the prioritised climate adaptation strategies in Nigeria (CBA, 2025). The relative
performance and attractiveness of the strategies were also ranked separately
using Benefit-Cost Ratios (BCRs) and Net Present Values (NPVs) as yardsticks
under both the 2050 and 2080 horizons.

2.8.3 Climate Mobility Analysis for the NAP

Climate mobility refers to the movement of people motivated by the adverse effects
of sudden- or slow-onset climate impacts. It occurs both within and across national
borders and involves varying levels of constraints, agency, and vulnerability,
encompassing various forms of movement, including forced displacement,
migration and planned relocation, as well as voluntary and involuntary immobility.
Climate mobility occurs over different distances and can be temporary, recurrent,


28   National Adaptation Plan (NAP)
 or permanent.

The inclusion of climate mobility in the NAP is based on an analysis of modelling
projections from the Africa Climate Mobility Initiative (ACMI), a partnership between
the African Union Commission, the World Bank, and the United Nations, supported
by the Global Centre for Climate Mobility (GCCM). Launched in 2021, the ACMI
aims to create a common evidence base and policy agenda to address climate-
forced migration and displacement in Africa while harnessing climate mobility to
strengthen the continent’s collective resilience and development (Amakrane et al.,
2023, p. 16). The ACMI used a gravity model, drawing on ISIMIP climate-impact data,
to project future shifts in population distribution under combined development
(SSP1, SSP3) and climate (RCP2.6, RCP6.0) scenarios, accounting for factors such
as flooding, crop and rangeland productivity, water security, sea-level rise, and
conflict.

The analysis of climate mobility for this NAP is further based on primary data
collected in the Ajegunle suburb of Lagos, a waterside informal settlement of
around 550,000 residents, mostly internal migrants, where research was conducted
in 2021, including 110 survey interviews and three focus group discussions (Mixed
Migration Centre, 2023). It also draws on a literature review of the existing academic
and grey literature on climate risks as a driver of human mobility in Nigeria, the
impacts of climate mobility on those who move and the communities involved, and
the consideration of the issue in existing policy frameworks (GCCM, 2026).

Reference to climate mobility in the NAP complements Nigeria’s inclusion of climate
mobility dynamics in other key climate strategies, such as the NDC 3.0, the Just
Transition Plan, and subnational plans such as Lagos’ Resilience strategy. It further
aligns Nigeria’s climate policy framework with the country’s obligations under the
Kampala Declaration on Internal Displacement and with commitments made in the
Kampala Ministerial Declaration on Migration, Environment and Climate Change
and the Global Principles for Addressing Climate Mobility. By including climate
mobility in the NAP, Nigeria can strengthen policy integration across sectors to
support positive adaptation journeys for some of its most vulnerable communities.
While most Nigerians are likely to have a strong attachment to their land and homes,
acknowledging and proactively supporting communities in exploring climate
mobility as an adaptation strategy will be critical for social cohesion and positive
community transition in the face of adverse climate impacts.

2.8.4 Gender Analysis for NAP

Vulnerability to climate change at different spatial levels is exacerbated by inequity
and marginalisation linked to gender, ethnicity, income, or combinations thereof
(high confidence), especially for many Indigenous Peoples and local communities



                                               National Adaptation Plan (NAP)      29
 (high confidence) (IPCC, 2023). Gender issues play a crucial role in shaping the
effectiveness and success of climate change adaptation strategies because women
and men have distinct roles and responsibilities in Nigeria; have limited access
to productive resources, including land, credit, and technology; and have limited
access to education and other economic benefits – which exacerbate pre-existing
inequalities and vulnerabilities, hampering women’s ability to adapt effectively to
climate change impacts (Akinbami et al., 2019; Chingarande et al., 2020). To this
end, Nigeria incorporated gender dynamics into the National Adaptation Plan
process to foster inclusive climate resilience, promote social justice, and ensure
sustainable development (Jangbrand, 2022; Dazé, 2020; Sriram, 2018; Nelson,
2015). The gender analysis adopted a desk review of relevant literature, national
policies, laws, strategies, and plans, and consultations with key stakeholders,
comprising state and non-state actors.

The gender analysis drew on the National Action Plan on Gender and Climate Change
(NAPGCC, FMEnv, 2020b) and on experiences recorded during the implementation
of gender-responsive climate actions in Nigeria and across the globe to identify
weaknesses and integrate country-specific recommendations. Nigeria still has a
great deal of work to do to achieve gender equality, given the strong influence of
cultural, religious, and traditional beliefs on gender norms and roles in the country.
It also took into account relevant existing policies in Nigeria, including: National
Climate Change Policy for Nigeria (2021-2030); Climate Change Act 2021; Nigeria’s
Adaptation Communication to the UFCCC (2021); NAPF (2020); LTV-2050; LT-

2.8.5 Conflict Sensitivity and Peace-Building in NAP

Climate change could lead to or exacerbate conflict through various cascading

sensitivity and peacebuilding into Nigeria’s National Adaptation Plan Process, with
support from the NAP Global Network (Annex 8). Understanding these cascading
impacts is crucial for developing effective adaptation strategies, reducing the risk
of conflict, and promoting peace and stability. The initiative began by integrating
conflict analysis tools and methods into the CRA approach, including participatory
risk assessments and the organisation of CRA fieldwork and conflict analysis
workshops in some States. Consultations and counselling were organised for the

3.1    Conceptual Framework

Nigeria is highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Consequently,
climate-related extreme weather events are severely affecting Nigeria’s economy.
The aim of the NAP process is to identify effective measures that will reduce the
country’s vulnerability to climate change and enhance its adaptive capacity across
sectors and communities, thereby protecting lives and livelihoods and sustaining
development gains. Given resource constraints, the NAP process is streamlined
to focus on priority sectors, including highly vulnerable sectors and cross-cutting
sectors such as agriculture, energy, health, water resources, ecosystems, and
biodiversity, as well as conflict-sensitive adaptation. Achieving the NAP goal
depends heavily on effective finance mobilisation, which could come from the
public sector, the private sector, international finance, or a blended finance
mechanism.

Phasing the implementation of the NAP into medium- and long-term strategies
supports financial mobilisation and strengthens national capacity to integrate
flexibility into the process. Cross-cutting themes such as gender, youth, indigenous
knowledge, disaster risk reduction, and governance were integrated to achieve
wider participation and ownership. Defining the institutional arrangements and
coordination framework is crucial for successful implementation and for achieving
the adaptation goals. Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV), with appropriate
indicators, is built into the NAP process, allowing tracking of progress and financial
flows. An effective monitoring and evaluation plan, with tools such as results-based
frameworks, is useful for periodic reviews, learning loops, and updating the NAP.
Reporting patterns, communication, and stakeholder engagement strategies are
also useful for successful planning and implementation of the NAP.

3.2    Boundary Conditions for the Assessment

Nigeria’s NAP process focuses on agriculture, water resources, and energy as the
priority sectors for adaptation actions. However, the process does not neglect the
high vulnerability and adaptation needs of other key economic sectors, such as


34    National Adaptation Plan (NAP)
 health, transport, commerce and industry, and education. The NAP also highlights
the relevance of other critical cross-cutting issues, such as women and gender
equality, youth, persons with disabilities, and private sector engagement. Relevant
strategies were identified on the basis of IPCC SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 and in
alignment with national aspirations. The national context was first examined in
relation to the physical implementation of the adaptation strategies, strengthening
institutional capacities, the need to mobilise resources, social inclusion and equity,
attracting transformational investments, and creating the enabling environment to
support the implementation of the NAP. Women, youth, older people, persons with
disabilities, ethnic communities, socially disadvantaged groups, and the private
sector are integral considerations across all sectors to ensure participatory NAP
implementation.

3.3 Synergy with SDGs, Sendai Framework for DRR, and other relevant
regional and national frameworks

Nigeria’s NAP aligns with and strongly complements the Sendai Framework 2015-
2030, whose goal is to “prevent new and reduce existing disaster risks through
the implementation of integrated and inclusive economic, structural, legal,
social, health, cultural, educational, environmental, technological, political and
institutional measures that prevent and reduce hazard exposure and vulnerability
to disaster, increase preparedness for response and recovery, and thus strengthen
resilience”. Nigeria further demonstrated its commitment to the Sendai Framework
by developing a National Disaster Risk Management Policy (NDRMP) in 2018 to
strengthen its capacity to reduce vulnerability, prevent the creation of new disaster
risks, and promote the accountability needed at all levels. The NAP approach is
consistent with objective 3 of the NDRMP, which aims to reduce the vulnerability
of the poor by building capacity and resilience to disaster risk.

Nigeria is committed to the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for 2015-
2030, which envision a future that is economically sustainable, socially inclusive
and environmentally resilient. Nigeria’s SDG framework was established through
the Nigeria Governor’s Forum. The NAP aligns with the 17 SDGs, which represent
a universal call to action to end poverty in all its forms, safeguard the planet and
ensure that all peoples enjoy peace and prosperity by 2030. It particularly aligns
with SDGs 1 (No Poverty), 2 (Zero Hunger), 5 (Gender Equality), 6 (Clean Water and
Sanitation), 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), and 13 (Climate Action). Nigeria’s NAP
is a national instrument for achieving these goals through adaptive pathways to
reach SDG targets by 2030. All the Adaptation Priorities emphasised in Nigeria’s
NAP directly or indirectly align with the SDGs’ strategic interventions.

3.4.4 Sea-level rise

Nigeria’s coastline, approximately 853 km long, is low-lying and highly vulnerable
to sea-level rise (Danladi et al., 2017; Oloyede et al., 2021). Even small increases in
sea level could have major effects and permanently alter coastlines. For coastal
ecosystems and communities, sea-level rise poses an additional threat of flooding.
This rise mostly stems from oceanic thermal expansion and the melting of
Antarctic ice, which could cause salinisation, flooding and erosion (IFO Institute
for Economic Research and Climate Analytics, 2021). As a result, low-lying coastal
areas are projected to be submerged by 2100 (Merem et al., 2019). Along its vast
coastlines, diverse forest ecosystems in the South, including the Niger Delta area
with its 1,900 km² mangrove swamps and cities within, have experienced climatic
hazards ranging from heavy rains to coastal inundation in recent decades (Merem
et al., 2019). Between 1960 and 1970, the southern coastline saw a sea-level rise
of 0.462 m, which resulted in the flooding of communities, the erosion of low-
lying areas, and the loss of mangroves, amid the growth of human settlements and
infrastructure (Merem et al., 2019). Baba et al. (2023) observed that the average
sea-level rise anomaly in Nigeria between 2015 and 2020 is 15.94 cm. Nigeria’s
coastline, originally endowed with a fragile mangrove system, has been depleted
over time due to human activities such as crude oil exploration, use of wood as fuel,
timber, fishing, sand mining, etc (Oloyede et al., 2021).

 3.5    Climate Risks and Vulnerabilities Projections

3.5.1 Climate scenarios projection

Future climate projections for Nigeria indicate significant warming and shifts in
precipitation patterns over the next century.

3.5.1.1 Expected temperature levels in variability (at medium and long term for
both national and agroecological zones)

Projections from two Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) – the high-
emission scenario (RCP 8.5) and the medium-emission scenario (RCP 4.5) – indicate
an increase in mean annual temperature across Nigeria (TNC), with increases
ranging from 1.48°C to 3.48°C in the near future (Federal Ministry of Environment,
2020). The CRA report, using the SSPs assessment, also shows changes in mean
annual temperature across all agroecological regions. The CRA (2025) projects
that Nigeria will experience significant warming under both RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5,
with warming of +2.5 to +3.2 °C by 2050.

3.5.1.2 Expected rainfall levels in variability (at medium and long term for both
national and agroecological zones)

Nigeria is likely to see changes in the number of heavy rainy days across the near-,
mid-, and long-term, with a strong projection of an average increase in the number
of heavy rainy days within the reference period under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5.
The CRA (2025) projects that Nigeria will experience significant rainfall variability
under both RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5, with more frequent heavy rainfall events. The
number of days with extreme rainfall (≥20 mm) is expected to increase by ~20% by
2080, raising concerns about a higher frequency of floods. Projections of future
increases in precipitation are particularly significant for the northern ecological
zones, such as the Sahel and Sudan savanna, from the near-term to the long-term.
An increase in the number of very heavy rainy days is likely to be recorded in the
country, with the lowest increase in the near-term and the highest in the long-term
under both SSPs.

Similarly, the Third National Communication (TNC) indicated a likely significant
increase in precipitation across the country up to 2070, with annual rainfall projected
to rise by 9 to 45.8%. In particular, the southern part of the country is projected to
see more areas with high annual rainfall, with seasons of up to 3000mm/year, and
rainfall expected to increase by 20 to 30mm per year in susceptible regions by
2050 under RCP 8.5 in Nigeria (Federal Ministry of Environment, 2020). This will
be due to the expected warmer atmosphere, which could hold more evaporated
water, making rainfall heavier and more intense and causing flash floods. A slight



42    National Adaptation Plan (NAP)
 increase in the number of extremely heavy rainy days from near-term to long-term
is expected under both SSPs, except for the long-term under SSP5-8.5, where
the increase is very large and spreads across all ecological zones (Figure 3.7).
Specifically, the Sahel and Guinea Savannah would likely see the highest increase in
the future (FMEnv-CRA 2025). There is also the likelihood of a decrease in the near-
term in the mangrove/swamp forest zone, where the highest number of extremely
rainy days occurred. One of the direct consequences of the increased occurrence
of heavy rain is flooding. The findings of the CRA report appear contrary to TNC
predictions under RCP 8.5, which indicate a significant decrease in rainfall (10-

Analytics, info Institute and Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, 2021).
Nevertheless, these projections would impact different socioeconomic sectors
such as agriculture, water resources, health, energy and so on.

Flood risk for the current period indicates that southern Nigeria is the area with the
highest flood risk. For the remaining parts of the country, areas with high flood risk
are those located near major rivers (Figure 3.6).

 3.5.2 Increased Extremities of Hazards

The major climate hazards experienced in the country include flooding, drought
and aridity, extreme heat waves, landslides and erosion, and sea-level rise. These
hazards have varying degrees of impact on the national economy. The occurrence
of these hazards is also projected to affect different sectors of the economy, as
well as communities and individuals, in the future.

3.5.2.1 Rain-induced flooding

Nigeria has experienced several major flood events in the past, with their frequency
and severity increasing over time. Nigeria’s coastal states face extensive risks
from storm surge along the entire coast, inland flooding and wildfires in the Niger
Delta region, and negative rainfall anomalies in the southeast. Notable flooding
events include those in 2012, 2015 and 2022. Severe flooding in 2012 affected
seven million people and caused economic damage estimated at $500 million,
while severe flooding in 2015 affected one million people and resulted in damage
of approximately $25 million (GERICS, 2015). The impact assessment of the 2022
flood showed extensive loss of life (with over 600 deaths), damage to livelihoods,
and the disruption of essential services and economic activities (National Bureau
of Statistics, National Emergency Management Agency and United Nations
Development Programme). The flood affected 4.4 million people across Nigeria,
including 2.6 million children, and some 2.4 million people were displaced (UNICEF,
2023). The Nigeria Bureau of Statistics reported in 2023 that the devastating
impact of the 2022 flood was in the range of US$3.79 billion to $9.12 billion (Oke
et al., 2023).

Climate change trends in Nigeria are expected to increase the risk and intensity
of flooding through more frequent and intense heavy rainfall events (Figure 3.8).
Future projections indicate an average increase in the number of heavy rainy days
from near-term to long-term across Nigeria, especially in the northern ecological
zone (Sahel and Sudan savannah). An increase in very heavy rainy days could
also be recorded in the country, with the lowest increase in the near-term and the
highest in the long-term under both SSPs (FNEnv-CRA, 2025). For extremely heavy
rainy days, Nigeria is expected to see a slight increase in the number of days from
near-term to long-term under both SSPs, except in the long-term under SSP5-8.5,
where the increase is very large and spreads across all ecological zones. Increases
in the number of extreme rainy days will directly lead to flooding.

Drought is a recurring event in Nigeria, particularly in many northern States, where

an expansion of the Sahara Desert by approximately 3600 square kilometres,
including the drying up of Lake Chad due to a southward shift in precipitation
(Haider, 2019; Hwang et al., 2013). The trend has been towards a generally drier
climate, which is worsening food insecurity in the country (Haider, 2019).

In 1972-1973, a severe drought (largely caused by decreasing rainfall) in the
Sudano-Sahelian areas of West Africa led to catastrophic loss of human life and
livestock (FMEnv, 2020). Ogunride et al. (2023) predicted an increase in drought
frequency and intensity in Nigeria. In their drought analysis under the RCP 8.5
scenario, the frequency of severe/extreme drought would intensify towards the
end of the 21st century. Water availability will be affected by possible periods of
drought (Ayanlade et al., 2018).

Rainfall has continued to decline since the 1970s to date. This period of drastic

periods of drought. Considering population growth for the country in the coming
years, water availability is projected to decrease by more than three-quarters –
from 3 300 m³ per capita in 2000 to about 800 m³ per capita in 2080 – below the
UN threshold for water scarcity (Climate Analytics, IFO Institute and Potsdam
Institute for Climate Impact Research, 2021) – making it increasingly difficult to
provide enough water to the entire population.

At the aggregate country level, soil moisture is projected to decline slightly by about
1.1% as 2080 approaches (Climate Analytics, IFO Institute and Potsdam Institute
for Climate Impact Research, 2021). However, regional disparities exist, and soil
aridity could increase by 10% in 2080 in some northern regions under the RCP6.0
scenario (Climate Analytics, IFO Institute and Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact
Research, 2021).

3.5.2.3 Variations in Sea-level rise

The current global estimate of sea- level rise is 0.2. 1m, with projections to
increase to 1. 32 m by the year 2100 and 5. 61 m by 2300 under the Representative
Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8. 5 (World Economic Forum, 2024; Horton et al.,
2020). This implies that, with the present 0. 2 m sea- level rise, the inundated area
of 3,400 km² in Nigeria’ s coastal regions will increase to 18,400 km² under the
projected 1 m scenario (Federal Republic of Nigeria, 2023). The projected sea- level
rise values based on the RCP 8. 5 scenario for the years 2025, 2050, 2075, and 2100
are 11. 92, 29. 07, 53. 09, and 84. 25 cm, respectively (Oloyede et al., 2021). Empirical
evidence suggests that 40. 1% to 58. 9% of the Niger Delta coastline is highly or
very highly vulnerable to sea- level rise (Dike et al., 2024). Coastal settlements
such as Bonny, Forcados, Lagos, Port Harcourt, Warri, and Calabar, which are less
than 10 m above sea level, will be seriously threatened by a 1 m sea- level rise
under SSP 5- 8. 5 (Federal Republic of Nigeria, 2023). Additionally, the country’s

 3.5.2.5 Landslides and erosion

Heavy rainfall could trigger landslides, mudslides, and consequently gully erosion
in sedimentary terrains. An increased incidence of extreme rainfall may also
result in soil erosion and waterlogging of crops, thereby decreasing yields and
increasing food insecurity. This may lead to significant economic losses, damage
to agricultural land and infrastructure, and human casualties. Land degradation
and soil erosion, exacerbated by recurrent flooding, adversely affect agricultural
production, disproportionately affecting the livelihoods of the rural poor. More
extreme weather events, such as intense rainfall after prolonged dry spells, can
lead to erosion and flash flooding, damaging roads and infrastructure, wiping out
crops, and putting additional lives at risk (USAID, 2018).

In 2015 and 2020, there were about 99.21 km2 and 148.77 km2 of gully erosion
sites, respectively, in southeast Nigeria – Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu, and Imo
States (Enemuoh et al., 2023). This represents a significant increase in the area
affected by gully erosion in the region. Enemuoh et al. (2023) projected that the area
affected by gully erosion in the region would increase to 172.65 km2 by 2030. This
prediction highlights the urgency of proactive measures to counteract the adverse
effects of gully erosion on the environment, infrastructure, and communities.
Anticipatory adaptation measures are therefore needed to respond to the threat
of gully erosion in Nigeria. Planning, resource allocation, policy formulation, and
collaborative efforts are needed to address the escalating threat of gully erosion
in South-East Nigeria.

Landslides are more pronounced in southern Nigeria than in the northern part of
the country. The loose nature of sedimentary rocks and gully erosion triggered by
heavy rainfall and subsequent flooding are the primary causes of most landslides in
southern Nigeria (Bamisaiye, 2019; Nnanwuba et al., 2022). Furthermore, Nnanwuba
et al. (2022) listed other factors and their levels of contribution to landslides in
southeastern Nigeria. These factors include rainfall (0.860), slope (0.566), aspect
(0.553), distance to fault (0.512), elevation (0.348), distance to drainage (0.333),
Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) (0.250), general curvature (0.117),
land use (0.074), and geology (0.038) (see Figure 7). Heavy rainfall is the main
factor contributing to landslides in the region. Heavy rainfall is also implicated in
gully erosion (Figure 3.17).

3.5.3 Climate stress areas

All sectors of the Nigerian economy, including various development initiatives, are
vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Natural, human, and physical assets
are vulnerable to climate change. Climate change affects the ability of Nigeria’s
natural capital to deliver its wide range of goods and services. Extreme weather
events negatively impact Nigerian cities, roads, drainage systems, power plants,
ports, and other types of infrastructure. Nigeria’s human capital is also threatened
by climate change, as it affects the ability to build and improve the country’s health
and education. For example, floods and heat waves affect children’s access to
school and hinder conducive learning.

Nigeria’s diverse ecological zones have created opportunities for multiple
livelihoods, agricultural practices, and commodities, all of which are affected by
climate change and shocks (Table 3.2). Vulnerability, which varies from region to
region, reflects existing variation in the climates and socioeconomic features of
Nigeria’s ecological regions. Rising sea levels threaten coastal communities, with
flooding, saltwater intrusion, and waterborne disease becoming more frequent.
Drought and aridity, combined with rising surface air temperatures, limit the
country’s hydropower systems in the north and frustrate agricultural production and


                                                        National Adaptation Plan (NAP)             55
 fishing, endangering food security and negatively impacting health and nutrition
(USAID, 2023). In the central and southern regions, high-intensity rainfall events
cause floods and erosion, resulting in significant loss and damage to infrastructure.
Floods and other climate-change-related hazards in Nigeria have also increased
the incidence of diseases, particularly malaria, which was responsible for about
200,000 deaths in 2021 in the country (WHO, 2022). A combination of frequent
climate-change-related hazards, a large population, poor infrastructure, poverty,
limited access to technologies, and low adaptive capacity heightens Nigeria’s
vulnerability.

3.5.3.1 Risks and vulnerabilities of different sectors
3.5.3.1.1 Agriculture

Agriculture is a significant contributor to Nigeria’s economy and food security. The
sector contributed 21.07% to the gross domestic product in the first quarter of
2024 and employed over 70% of Nigerians (FAO, 2024; NBS, 2024). Over 80% of
Nigerian farmers are smallholders, accounting for 90% of the country’s agricultural
production, yet they have limited access to improved production technologies and
mechanisation (Oyaniran, 2020). Nigeria’s agricultural land area is about 686,440
km2, representing 75.4% of the country’s total land area (World Bank Group,
2024c; World Bank Group, 2024d). The country’s agriculture can be divided into
four sectors: crop production (accounting for around 87.6% of the sector’s total
output) – with cash and food (or subsistence) crops – livestock (8.1%), fishing
(3.2%) and forestry (1.1%) (Oyaniran, 2020). Gender roles in Nigeria’s agricultural
sector are often differentiated, with men mainly involved in ploughing, planting,
and the more lucrative cash crops, while women are more often involved in growing
food crops, processing agricultural products, and marketing surpluses. Although
women have limited access to resources such as land and credit, they still make a
significant contribution to Nigeria’s food security by growing subsistence crops and
participating in post-harvest activities such as storing and processing agricultural
products.

3.5.3.1.1.1 Crop production

Nigeria’s agricultural production covers almost 70 million hectares, with diverse food
crops cultivated by farmers, including rice, maize, yam, cocoyam, beans, sorghum,
millet, melon, and soya beans, which are mainly grown by small-scale farmers
(FAO, 2024a). The most widespread food crops are maize and cassava, grown by
almost 50% of households, while cocoyam and sesame beni-seeds are grown by
7.7% and 3.6% of Nigerian households, respectively (Figure 3.18). Important cash
crops grown in the country include cocoa, palm oil, rubber, groundnut, and cotton.

Nigeria’s agricultural sector faces a myriad of problems, including poor soil fertility,
land fragmentation, an inefficient tenure system, a weak agricultural extension
system, low adoption of improved technologies, substantial post-harvest losses,
and limited access to inputs and finance, all of which contribute to low productivity
in the sector. Climate change exacerbates these challenges. Agricultural yields in
Nigeria are increasingly at risk from climate change, as shifting weather patterns,
rising temperatures, and more frequent extreme events such as droughts and floods
disrupt crop production cycles. Climate change affects agricultural production
in several ways. Currently, erratic rainfall and prolonged dry seasons limit water
availability for crops, while rising temperatures stress plant growth, reduce soil
moisture, and increase evapotranspiration, leaving crops and livestock vulnerable.
Unpredictable rainfall complicates farmers’ planning and shortens the cropping
season and growing days. Numerous crops are susceptible to even minor variations
in rainfall and temperature.

The cascading impacts of these changes affect the population’s livelihoods
and threaten food security, as lower agricultural yields directly affect Nigeria’s
food supply, increase prices, and reduce household incomes, especially among
smallholder farmers who rely heavily on seasonal harvests (Figure 3.19). Nigerian
agriculture is mainly rain-fed (less than 1% is irrigated) and is therefore intrinsically
sensitive to climatic hazards. Farmers are also particularly vulnerable due to limited
access to irrigation, climate-resilient seeds, and crop insurance, all of which could
buffer against climate impacts.

Increased heat and drought in the Northeast have been linked to crop failures
and declines in agricultural output. Along the Southern coast, rising sea levels
are flooding cropland, making soils unsuitable for planting, and in the Southeast,
erosion is further reducing yields. This vulnerability is compounded by insufficient


                                                       National Adaptation Plan (NAP)         57
 infrastructure, such as storage facilities to protect crops during extreme weather,
and by inadequate access to financial resources and technical assistance that could
help farmers adapt. As climate change progresses, Nigeria’s agricultural sector
may face heightened economic losses, increased poverty, and food insecurity, all
of which threaten broader socio-economic stability in the country.

3.5.3.1.1.2 Livestock

Livestock production in Nigeria is a crucial component of the agricultural sector and
plays a significant role in the country’s economy and food security. The livestock
sector contributes about 17% to Nigeria’s agricultural GDP and 5% to the national
GDP (ILRI, 2023). Nigeria’s livestock sub-sector includes the production of poultry
(180 million), goats (76 million), sheep (43.4 million), cattle (18.4 million) and pigs
(7.5 million) (FAO, 2021). The vulnerability factors and primary impacts are shown
in Figure 3.20.




58   National Adaptation Plan (NAP)
 Figure 3.20: Cascading Impacts of climate hazards on livestock production


Nigeria’s livestock sector faces significant and growing risks from climate change,
primarily from rising temperatures, unpredictable rainfall patterns, prolonged
droughts, and extreme weather events such as floods. Higher temperatures and
increased heat stress reduce livestock productivity by affecting health, fertility,
and milk production, while prolonged droughts deplete water sources and degrade
grazing land, leading to poor-quality fodder. Droughts also limit access to critical
feed resources, weakening livestock health and increasing mortality rates. As
droughts become more frequent, they reduce pasture availability and force herders
to travel greater distances in search of water, increasing the likelihood of conflict
over resources, particularly between pastoralists and farmers in northern Nigeria.
Weight loss in animals can reduce meat and dairy production. Additionally, floods
damage infrastructure, contaminate water sources, and spread diseases such as
foot-and-mouth disease, further stressing livestock populations. Key cascading
impacts on the national economy include increased prices of animal products, job
losses across the livestock value chain, reduced income, increased rural-to-urban
migration, and shortages of livestock products in the market.

Figure 3.20 shows the key vulnerability factors, including reliance on rain-fed
grazing lands and traditional herding practices; lack of adaptive infrastructure,
such as drought-resilient pasture management and efficient water storage
systems; limited access to veterinary services and to climate-adapted breeds
that are more resistant to heat stress and disease; low financial resources; limited
access to technology; and inadequate support for livestock farmers.

 3.5.3.1.2 Fishery

Nigeria is the second-largest producer of farmed fish on the continent and the fifth-
largest consumer. Fishing enterprises operate across a range of habitats nationwide,
including marine, brackish and freshwater, with most activity concentrated along
Nigeria’s 960-km coastline. About 90% of fish produced in Nigeria is sold in local
markets, partly constituting 40% of the country’s dietary protein consumption
for the growing population (Tokpo, 2024, CRA, 2025). With an estimated annual
fish demand of 2.0 million metric tons, only about 42.5% is met by domestic
production; the rest is supplemented by fish imports (Idowu et al., 2011). Nigeria’s
domestic fisheries production comprises four main segments: artisanal (coastal)
fishing, which contributes 80%; industrial coastal (trawl) fishing, 10%; artisanal
inland fishing, 6%; and aquaculture, 4% (Idowu et al., 2011). In 2022, 613,800 people
were employed in inland fishing, of which 27% were women; 120,000 in sea fishing,
of which 20% were women; and 13,600 in aquaculture, of which 2% were women
(FAO, 2024b). Aquaculture has received a boost from private-sector investment in
recent years, making Nigeria a major producer in Sub-Saharan Africa. However,
this sub-sector is increasingly affected by climate change and further hampered
by inherent vulnerabilities.




Figure 3.21 Cascading Impacts of climate hazards on fishery sector


The country’s fisheries sector faces immediate and future climate risks from
rising water temperatures, altered rainfall patterns, ocean acidification, sea-level
rise, and more frequent extreme weather events. Figure 3.21 indicates that rising
water temperatures, which affect both inland and marine fisheries, will disrupt the
natural habitats and migratory patterns of fish species, alter reproductive cycles,
and push certain species towards extinction or force them to migrate to cooler


60   National Adaptation Plan (NAP)
 waters. Unpredictable rainfall patterns and prolonged dry seasons are altering the
flow of rivers and lakes, disrupting breeding grounds, particularly for freshwater
fish, and resulting in seasonal water scarcity. Ocean acidification, caused by
increased carbon dioxide absorption, is reducing the availability of calcium
carbonate, essential for shellfish and coral growth. This degrades coral reefs and
other critical habitats that serve as breeding and feeding grounds for various
fish species, thereby affecting fish populations. Rising sea levels exacerbate
these challenges by causing saltwater intrusion in coastal and freshwater areas,
making certain habitats unsuitable for freshwater species and harming the fishing
communities that depend on these ecosystems. Extreme weather events, such as
storms and floods, damage fishing infrastructure, from boats to ports, and increase
sedimentation in water bodies, reducing water quality and causing fish kills due to
oxygen depletion.

Other key vulnerabilities of the fishery sector include (i) limited access to modern
equipment, advanced fish-finding technologies, and sustainable fishing methods
among the traditional and artisanal fishing population, who constitute the majority in
the sector; (ii) overfishing driven by high demand and weak regulatory enforcement,
which weakens fish populations and reduces their resilience to climate stressors;
and (iii) limited access to climate data and early warning systems, which would
otherwise help inform decisions about safe fishing times and locations (Figure
3.21). Overall, the impacts on Nigeria’s economy include decreased fish stocks,
higher prices for fish products, loss of livelihoods for many fishing-dependent
communities, and greater food insecurity across Nigeria, posing a substantial
threat to both local economies and national food supply chains.

3.5.3.1.3 Forestry

Nigeria has a valuable forest stock that covered 7.7% of the country’s land area
in 2015. The forest sector contributes about 2.5% to the Gross Domestic Product
and employs around 5 million people through the supply of timber and non-timber
forest products (NTFP) (UNEP, n.d.). These forests provide important ecosystem
goods and services for the population, including forest-based farming, household
equipment, furniture and building materials, timber logging, fuel wood for cooking
or charcoal production, fodder (grasses and leaves for livestock), materials for
craft, medicinal plants, NTFP, including leaves, honey and fruit, as well as hunting
of animals (Fadairo et al., 2017). According to Nigeria’s Fifth National Biodiversity
Report, 70% of Nigerian households and 90% of the country’s rural population use
firewood for their energy needs (UNEP, n.d.). Nigeria’s forest resources are divided
into five distinct ecological zones, namely: the freshwater and mangrove ecological
zones, the lowland rainforest, the derived savannah, the Guinean savannah and the
Sudan and Sahel ecological zone. There are also a few strips of mountain forest on
the plateaux and highlands (Federal Ministry of Environment, Nigeria, 2020). The


                                               National Adaptation Plan (NAP)      61
 Niger Delta in southern Nigeria has the largest mangrove system in Africa, with an
estimated 1 million hectares (UNEP, n.d.).

Of an estimated 10 million hectares (about 10% of Nigeria’s surface area) originally
set aside as forest reserves and conservation areas, only 6% of the total area
remains, partly due to deforestation, forest land degradation, climate change and
infrastructural development (Federal Ministry of Environment, Nigeria, 2020).
Protected areas in Nigeria include 994 forest reserves, 7 national parks, 32 game
reserves and sanctuaries, 11 Ramsar sites, 27 Important Bird Areas, 2 World Heritage
sites and 5 biosphere reserves.

Climate change poses a significant current and future risk to the forest sector in
Nigeria, exacerbating existing challenges such as deforestation, illegal logging,
and land conversion for agriculture. As shown in the figure below, increased
temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and more frequent extreme weather
events have complex, cascading impacts on forest ecosystems, biodiversity, and
human communities, both in the immediate term and over the long term.




Figure 3.22 Cascading Impacts of climate hazards on forestry resources

Rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns are stressing some tree
species, disrupting their growth cycles, reducing their resilience, and causing
shifts in forest ecosystems. Prolonged droughts are worsening these conditions,
drying out soils and increasing tree mortality, particularly among species that
depend on consistent rainfall. This loss of vegetation cover also exposes soils
to erosion, reduces soil fertility, and diminishes forests’ ability to regenerate,
which can lead to gradual desertification, particularly in the northern regions of
Nigeria. Increased wildfires, fuelled by drier conditions and accumulated dead
vegetation, are causing widespread forest destruction, releasing vast amounts of


62    National Adaptation Plan (NAP)
 carbon dioxide and accelerating biodiversity loss by damaging habitats critical to
various plant and animal species. Sea-level rise is another factor affecting coastal
mangrove forests, as saltwater intrusion damages the roots and structure of these
ecosystems, weakening their role as protective barriers against coastal erosion
and as nurseries for marine life.

These cascading impacts severely reduce the productivity and resilience of the
forest sector, threatening the ecosystem services forests provide, such as water
regulation, carbon sequestration and soil protection, all of which are vital to
Nigeria’s environmental and economic stability (Figure 3.22). These climate risks
are compounded by the sector’s inherent vulnerabilities, including high rates
of deforestation driven by unsustainable logging, agricultural expansion and
firewood collection. Unsustainable practices not only reduce forest cover but also
weaken the adaptive capacity of forest ecosystems by disrupting biodiversity and
ecosystem resilience, making forests more vulnerable to the impacts of climate
change. In addition, the sector’s adaptive capacity is limited by weak enforcement
and a lack of community involvement in forest management, leading to unchecked
illegal logging and inadequate reforestation efforts. Many rural communities rely
heavily on forests for their livelihoods, from timber and fuelwood to non-timber
forest products, creating a high level of dependency that is difficult to shift
without viable economic alternatives. Limited financial resources and access to
climate-resilient forest management practices also hamper efforts to develop
adaptation strategies, such as reforestation with drought-resistant species or
the establishment of community-managed protected areas. As climate change
accelerates, Nigeria’s forest sector is at risk of significant degradation, which
would undermine local economies, reduce biodiversity, increase carbon emissions
and reduce natural defences against climate impacts such as erosion and flooding.
This degradation not only threatens the forest sector but also has wider socio-
economic and environmental impacts, as forest loss will reduce the resilience
of surrounding communities and ecosystems, leading to increased vulnerability
across the country.

3.5.3.1.4 Water Resources

Nigeria is endowed with a diversity of water systems, with significant regional
variations due to the country’s climatic zones and geography, ranging from the
arid Sahel in the north to the humid tropical rainforests in the south. These include
substantial annual rainfall, large surface water bodies, rivers, streams and lakes, as
well as plentiful reserves of groundwater. The Niger and Lake Chad Basins are the
two most prominent water systems in the country, though several smaller coastal
river basins exist. In addition to these two major basins, Nigeria also includes the
South-western and South-eastern littoral basins, which play a significant role in
the country’s hydrology.

Despite these resources, Nigeria remains vulnerable because the water supply is
unable to meet domestic, industrial and agricultural demand in recent times. A very
large proportion of the population is at risk of water stress, as less than 40% have
direct access to drinking water. Climate change is leading to increased variability
in precipitation, causing flooding in certain wetlands in the south of the country
and reduced rainfall in the savannahs of the north, which may lead to droughts and
a reduction in surface water resources in the north.

As the country’s population rises to 258 million by 2030, with a commensurate
increase in demand for food, demand for agricultural water is expected to rise.
National water consumption for irrigation in Nigeria stood at 1926 MCM/day (million
cubic metres per year) in 2010 and will rise to 6245 MCM/day (million cubic metres
per year) in 2030. About 88% of rural Nigerian households use surface water, and
83% of these households are among the poorest in the country (Abubakar, 2019).
The demand for municipal water in Nigeria will also rise to 8,852 MCM/year (million
cubic metres per year), which represents 53% of Nigeria’s total water demand
by 2030, or 16,585 MCM/year (Ojo et al., 2020). This situation is already putting
considerable pressure on Nigeria’s water resources, and the effects of climate
change will only exacerbate the problem further (Ojo et al., 2020).

Water resources in Nigeria face serious and growing risks from climate change,
driven by rising temperatures, shifting rainfall patterns, more frequent droughts
and floods, and other climate-induced phenomena.

Changing rainfall patterns are causing water scarcity in many regions, particularly
in the northern parts of the country, where dry seasons are becoming longer and
more intense, reducing river flows and groundwater recharge. Higher temperatures
increase evaporation from surface water sources such as rivers, lakes and
reservoirs, further reducing available water supplies while increasing demand from
agriculture, industry and households.

Droughts, exacerbated by climate change, reduce access to water for drinking,
irrigation and livestock, affecting food security and rural livelihoods, particularly in
the northern part of the country. Meanwhile, in southern and coastal areas, rising
sea levels are causing saltwater intrusion into freshwater aquifers, contaminating
vital water sources for people and agriculture. Intense rainfall and flooding events,
worsened by climate change, are overwhelming drainage systems and damaging
water infrastructure, contaminating drinking water sources with pollutants and
increasing the spread of waterborne diseases across all ecological zones of
Nigeria. The health and sanitation sector faces significant challenges because of
water shortages, with some communities still practising open defecation.

The cascading impacts not only limit access to safe and clean water but also increase
the burden on public health systems, reduce agricultural productivity, and drive up
costs for water treatment and infrastructure repairs (Figure 3.23). These climate-
related water challenges are exacerbated by Nigeria’s inherent vulnerabilities, such
as (i) indiscriminate waste disposal, (ii) poor management of water resources, (iii)
dependence on rain-fed agriculture and over-reliance on surface water resources,
and (iv) limited access to infrastructure for efficient water storage and distribution,
particularly in rural and underserved urban areas. In addition, rapid population growth

 and urbanisation are increasing demand for water, putting additional pressure on
already strained water systems and accelerating the depletion of both surface
and groundwater resources. The adaptive capacity of Nigeria’s water sector is also
limited by inadequate community awareness, lack of access to climate-resilient
technologies, inadequate investment in resilient infrastructure such as reservoirs,
pipelines and treatment plants, and the lack of comprehensive water management
to address issues such as equitable water allocation and groundwater regulation.
As climate change progresses, these vulnerabilities will worsen, leading to higher
incidences of water scarcity, contamination and infrastructure failure, which in turn
will exacerbate social inequalities, increase poverty and threaten food security.

3.5.3.1.5 Health

Nigeria’s health system and infrastructure are highly vulnerable to climate hazards.
In Nigeria, climate change is not only exacerbating existing health problems but
also compounding them through deficiencies in water and sanitation, energy
availability, waste management and food systems (FMH&SW, 2024). Climate
change also threatens health services, water and food security, infrastructure and
social protection frameworks.

According to Nigeria’s Climate Change and Health Vulnerability and Adaptation
(V&A) Assessment Report, published in October 2024, the severity and scale
of climate change-related health impacts are expected to worsen across all
geographical areas of the country. The report shows that, under all scenarios,
the risks associated with climate change in the country will increase, straining
healthcare capacity, increasing the vulnerability of communities, and creating
conditions conducive to the spread of disease.

Nigeria will experience a 21% increase in disease burden due to climate change
by 2030, with significant increases in water-borne diseases, non-communicable
diseases and mental health disorders (Nigeria Climate Change and Health, 2024).
The level of risk and impact varies by population and geographical zone. The
assessment also identifies children, the elderly and pregnant women as being
at increased risk from climate impacts, while the north-east and north-west
of Nigeria are likely to be more affected. Nigeria still has a high prevalence of
communicable diseases and a growing number of non-communicable diseases.
Communicable diseases (malaria, acute respiratory infections (ARI), measles,
diarrhoea, tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS and neglected tropical diseases) account
for 66% of the total burden of disease in the country. An estimated 97% of the
country’s population of 160 million is at risk of malaria, with children and pregnant
women most vulnerable to malaria-related illness and death in Nigeria. Similarly,
the burden of non-communicable diseases (e.g. cardiovascular disorders, diabetes,
cancers and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) remains a major challenge in

health problem in Nigeria and remain the underlying cause of 53% of under-five
mortality in the country.

Climate change exacerbates these health challenges and will continue to do so as
climate hazards intensify.

As climate change intensifies, the cascading impacts are becoming more severe

Rising temperatures, erratic rainfall patterns, and an increase in extreme weather
events are driving a surge in heat-related illnesses, respiratory conditions,
waterborne infections, and vector-borne diseases. Higher temperatures contribute
to heat stress and worsen cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, particularly in
densely populated urban areas where access to cooling infrastructure is limited.
Changes in rainfall patterns and warmer climates also create favourable conditions
for the spread of vector-borne diseases such as malaria and dengue fever, as
mosquitoes and other disease-carrying vectors thrive and expand their habitats
into regions previously less affected. More frequent and intense flooding, coupled
with inadequate sanitation systems, heightens the risk of waterborne diseases
such as cholera, typhoid, and dysentery, especially in vulnerable communities with
limited access to clean water and proper sanitation. Prolonged droughts further

 reduce water availability and quality, exacerbating malnutrition and dehydration,
which weaken immune systems and increase susceptibility to illness.

Key vulnerabilities in Nigeria’s health sector include (i) limited access to healthcare
in rural areas, (ii) shortages of medical supplies and personnel, and reliance on
unreliable energy sources that undermine the effectiveness of cooling systems,
water and sanitation, and disease prevention efforts; and (iii) limited investment
in climate-resilient infrastructure, such as flood-proof health facilities, robust
emergency response systems, and early warning mechanisms for disease
outbreaks (Figure 3.24). A lack of public health education on climate risks also
leaves communities ill-prepared to address climate-related health challenges. As
climate change intensifies, these vulnerabilities are expected to worsen, leading
to longer and more severe health crises that strain the sector’s capacity to deliver
timely and effective care.

3.5.3.1.6 Energy

Nigeria’s main sources of energy include oil and gas, and biomass. Nigeria is
Africa’s largest producer of crude oil, the world’s 14th-largest oil producer, and the
6th-largest exporter of liquefied natural gas (U.S. EIA, 2020). Despite being one of
the world’s largest oil producers, access to reliable electricity remains limited, with
only 55% of the population having access in 2020 (Environmental and Economic
Resource Centre, 2024). In particular, most rural communities remain off-grid and
are trapped in an energy-poverty loop. Most of the energy produced and exported
comes from oil and gas, whose coastal production is vulnerable to sea-level rise,
storm surges and coastal flooding.

 Nigeria’s energy sector is increasingly vulnerable to climate change and faces
immediate and long-term climate risks from rising temperatures, unpredictable
rainfall patterns and extreme weather events that affect energy production,
distribution and demand. Hydropower, which provides about 22% of Nigeria’s
electricity, is particularly sensitive to changes in rainfall and river flows. Prolonged
dry spells reduce water levels in rivers and reservoirs, thereby lowering hydropower
generation capacity. Rising temperatures increase electricity demand, particularly
for cooling in urban areas, putting additional strain on the grid and forcing an
increase in energy imports or reliance on inefficient back-up generators that are
costly and often run on fossil fuels. Higher temperatures also reduce the efficiency
of thermal power plants, which are another key component of Nigeria’s energy mix.
Cooling systems in these plants become less effective at higher temperatures,
reducing output and increasing operating costs. Extreme weather events, such
as storms and floods, exacerbate these risks by damaging energy infrastructure,
including transmission lines, substations and pipelines, resulting in widespread
service disruptions and costly repairs. Flooding, particularly in coastal and riverine
areas, can lead to erosion and the collapse of infrastructure, while increasing
sedimentation in reservoirs, reducing storage capacity and hydropower efficiency
over time.

and have limited access to alternative energy sources, thereby exacerbating

to worsen, leading to reduced energy security, higher costs for consumers, and
an increased burden on industries that rely on a consistent supply of electricity.

reduce industrial productivity, and exacerbate poverty and social inequality.

3.5.3.1.7 Transport

Though Nigeria has significantly developed road, air, rail and water transport,
the road transport system is dominant for moving goods and services across the
country and accounting for 86.4% of the national GDP in 2016. With an estimated
road network of 195,000 km, the country’s road network has been ranked the largest
in West Africa and the second largest south of the Sahara (Federal Republic of
Nigeria, 2020). The road infrastructure is poorly maintained particularly in the rural
communities, making them susceptible to flood events while many of the roads
witness traffic congestion due to inadequacy of the infrastructure especially in
the urban areas.

Nigeria’s rail system is relatively underdeveloped compared to other countries;
however, the ongoing modernization efforts to improve this sub-sector is
expected to ease congestion on the roads and provide a more sustainable mode of
transportation. The rail networks remain limited to certain regions, and flooding is
a challenge to rail tracks and disrupt Services.

The country’s waterways, which span about 8,600 km, are another essential
transport mode. Rivers like the Niger and Benue are key for moving bulk cargoes,
particularly to inland areas. Yet, flooding can lead to the disruption of inland
navigation routes, making goods transport vulnerable, especially during the peak
of rainy seasons.

The transport sector in Nigeria is increasingly vulnerable to the impacts of climate
change, with significant risks posed by rising temperatures, erratic rainfall
patterns, sea-level rise, and more frequent extreme weather events, all of which
disrupt transport infrastructure, services, and mobility. Rising temperatures are
accelerating the degradation of road surfaces, causing asphalt to soften and
crack, particularly in areas with outdated or poorly maintained infrastructure. This
degradation raises maintenance costs, shortens the lifespan of roads, bridges, and
railways, and complicates transport logistics. Intense and unpredictable rainfall
frequently leads to flooding, particularly in low-lying urban and coastal regions
such as Lagos, where drainage systems are often insufficient (Figure 3.26). Flooding
erodes soil, undermining road foundations and increasing the risk of landslides,
which leads to extended road closures and traffic disruptions. In addition, rising
sea levels and coastal erosion threaten Nigeria’s port infrastructure, with saltwater
intrusion corroding metal structures and compromising the stability of docks and
jetties, thereby affecting the flow of goods.

Extreme weather events, such as storms and heatwaves, disrupt air travel by
delaying flights and airport operations, increasing operating costs and affecting
air safety. Vulnerabilities within Nigeria’s transport sector only amplify these
risks. Much of the infrastructure is ageing, lacks resilience to climate change,
and is concentrated in areas highly exposed to climate hazards. The transport
sector’s heavy reliance on road transport, which handles over 80% of goods and
passengers, means that road disruptions significantly affect national mobility and
economic stability.

Limited financial resources further constrain the sector’s ability to invest in
resilient infrastructure or to improve drainage systems to mitigate flood damage.

enforcement, which hinders proactive measures such as strengthening coastal
defences around ports or elevating roadbeds in flood-prone areas. Rural areas, with
their limited transport infrastructure, are particularly vulnerable, as disruptions
often leave these regions isolated and hinder access to essential services. As
climate change intensifies, these vulnerabilities will worsen, leading to greater
infrastructure damage, higher maintenance costs, and longer service disruptions.
These effects will ripple through the economy, limit social mobility, and reduce
resilience to future climate impacts. These compounded challenges highlight the
urgent need for climate-adaptive transport policies and resilient infrastructure
investments to safeguard Nigeria’s transport sector in the face of a changing
climate.

3.5.3.1.8 Human Mobility

Climate change is reshaping patterns of human mobility and population distribution
across Nigeria, generating a complex spectrum of outcomes that range from forced
displacement to involuntary immobility. As the NAP’s analysis of climate impacts
across Nigeria’s ecological zones reveals, displacement risk related to climate
stressors is not uniformly distributed. It is concentrated in frontline communities
exposed to climate impacts and among populations whose livelihoods depend
on climate-sensitive resources and who face compounding socio-economic and
governance vulnerabilities.

 3.5.3.1.8.1 Regional Climate Stressors and Mobility Pressures

Nigeria’s diverse geography exposes different regions to distinct but interconnected
climate hazards. In the north, advancing desertification, prolonged droughts,
extreme heat, and land degradation (Agu et al., 2020; Vande, 2025) are progressively
reducing the availability of grazing land and freshwater resources, undermining
agropastoral livelihoods that support millions of people. In southern and coastal
areas, sea-level rise, intensifying rainfall variability, coastal erosion, and recurrent
flooding threaten settlements, infrastructure, and coastal economies (Ndimele et
al., 2024; Nkwunonwo et al., 2020; Yusuf, 2019; Obiefuna, 2021; Amakrane et al.,
2023). Across the country, more frequent and severe extreme weather events are
disrupting the agricultural calendar and eroding productive assets, pushing climate
mobility from a historically adaptive strategy toward an increasingly reactive and
distressed response.

3.5.3.1.8.2 Populations at Heightened Risk
If vulnerability to climate risks is unevenly distributed and shaped by livelihood
dependence, socio-economic status, past and ongoing displacement experiences,
gender, age, and geographic exposure, the following groups face particularly acute
risks:

        face livelihood collapse as water and grazing resources contract, driving
        southward mobility into the Middle Belt and Benue River Basin and
        heightening conflict risk with farming communities (Udoh et al., 2025; Agu

      Coastal communities: Densely populated coastal settlements, particularly

3.5.3.1.8.3 Trapped Populations and Involuntary Immobility

A critical but often overlooked dimension of climate risk is involuntary immobility:
the situation of households that wish to move but lack the financial, social, or
institutional resources to do so. Evidence from Ajegunle, Lagos, indicates that
nearly half of the surveyed residents expressed a desire to relocate but were
unable to finance the move (Mixed Migration Centre, 2023). In conflict-affected
areas of the Middle Belt, immobility may also reflect deep attachments to ancestral
land and collective identity, meaning that some populations remain in high-risk
environments not solely due to material constraints but also due to culturally
grounded decisions (Olumba, 2024; 2025). In both cases, immobile populations
remain exposed to escalating climate hazards without viable adaptation pathways.

3.5.3.1.8.4 The Climate–Conflict–Mobility Nexus

In northern and central Nigeria, climate mobility interacts with conflict dynamics
in ways that amplify overall vulnerability. Environmental degradation has been
documented to intensify competition over land, water, and pasture, fracturing
traditional conflict-resolution mechanisms, and, in some contexts, contributing to
recruitment into armed groups (Albert, 2025; Vande, 2025; Udoh et al., 2025; Agu
et al., 2020; Obioha, 2008). Farmer–herder conflicts in the Middle Belt represent
a particularly significant hotspot, where ecological pressures, displacement,
contested land tenure and identity-based tensions converge.

Poorly designed adaptation interventions—including large-scale infrastructure
projects and coastal protection schemes—may also generate displacement
(Rice et al., 2021; Ajibade, 2017) if communities are relocated without adequate
consultation, compensation, or livelihood support, further creating maladaptive
outcomes that deepen existing inequalities.

3.5.3.2 Future Climate Mobility Projections

By 2050, modelling projections by the Africa Climate Mobility Initiative (ACMI)
(Amakrane et al. 2023) suggest that up to 1.5% of Nigeria’s total population — or 6.6
million people — could be forced to move internally due to climate impacts under a
high-emissions, unequal development scenario (the “Rocky Road” RCP 6.0/SSP3).
Under a high-emissions, inclusive development scenario (the “High Road” RCP 6.0/

These projections indicate that when development is unequal (SSP3)—including

3.5.3.1.8.6 Stock-Taking: Policies, Practices, and Governance

Several existing policy frameworks acknowledge the growing impact of climate
change on human mobility in Nigeria. The National Climate Change Policy
(2021–2030) highlights increasing climate-driven mobility, particularly through a
security lens. The third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) goes further,
recognising emerging climate mobility patterns and calling for a standardised
definition of climate migration while explicitly embracing mobility as an adaptation
strategy. At the subnational level, Lagos State has identified planned relocation as
a component of climate resilience in its Climate Adaptation and Resilience Plan
(LCARP).

Despite these foundations, Nigeria’s approach to climate mobility remains
fragmented. No overarching policy framework currently harmonises priorities
across sectors, institutions, or levels of government, or positions mobility
systematically as part of the national climate resilience effort. This NAP addresses

it establishes clear policy objectives that identify Nigeria’s climate mobility

frontline communities.

3.5.4.1 Swamp Forest Zone

The swamp forest region of Nigeria is a unique and ecologically rich zone
characterised by dense mangroves, freshwater swamps, and flood-prone areas
along the lower Niger Delta and the coast. It spans 5 States (Akwa Ibom, Bayelsa,
Cross River, Delta and Rivers States). The vegetation of the swamp forest region
consists of four ecological zones: coastal forests, mangrove forests, freshwater
swamp forests and lowland rainforests. This ecological zone is characterised
by high annual rainfall, ranging from 2,000 mm to over 3,000 mm. The climate is
consistently warm, with average temperatures between 26-28°C, and is marked by
mild winds. The geography and economy of the region are deeply intertwined with
the swamp forest ecosystem. Communities depend heavily on fishing, small-scale
agriculture, and forest resources, all of which are influenced by the region’s unique
hydrological and ecological characteristics (Tables 3 and .4). Agricultural practices
in the zone are heavily influenced by abundant water resources, with a focus on
fishing and aquaculture.

 3.5.4.3 Guinea Savannah

The Guinea Savannah is Nigeria’s most extensive agroecological zone, covering

also favour livestock rearing, making it a significant belt for both crop and animal

3.5.4.4 Sudan Savannah

The Sudan Savannah of Nigeria is a flat, high-rainfall plain with lush green vegetation,
neither a rainforest nor a semi-desert such as the Sahel Zone. It is a dry Savannah
woodland where trees and grasses co-exist, making it well suited to animal and
crop production. The climate is marked by a wet season from May to September,
with annual rainfall ranging between 500 and 1000 mm. Sudan Savannah covers
Adamawa, Yobe, Zamfara, Kebbi, Gombe, Katsina, Kano, Bauchi, and Jigawa States.
The dry season extends from October to April, with high temperatures averaging
between 25°C and 35°C. The region is mostly inhabited by peasant farmers without
formal training in modern farming techniques. These farmers form a significant
percentage of the farming population in Nigeria. The Sudan Savannah is the
major source of grains (millet, wheat, maize, etc.) and livestock in Nigeria (Ugwu
et al., 2023). Its distinct wet and dry seasons make it particularly vulnerable to the
adverse effects of climate change, such as desertification, erratic rainfall patterns,
and an increased frequency of extreme weather events (Table 3.7).

 3.5.4.5 Sahel

The Sahel Zone in Nigeria forms a transitional belt between the arid Sahara Desert
and the humid Sudan Savannah. This agroecological zone is found mainly in the
country’s northernmost states: Sokoto, Zamfara, Yobe and Borno, with a significant
presence in Katsina, Jigawa and Kebbi States. The Sahel agroecological zone is
characterised by a semi-arid climate, sparse vegetation and highly variable rainfall,
with an annual average of 500 mm (Nicholson, 2013) at its southern limits. The
region’s vegetation consists predominantly of drought-resistant species, including
grasses, thorny shrubs, and scattered acacia and baobab trees (Table 3.8). Seasonal
watercourses known as wadis provide temporary water resources during the brief
rainy season but remain dry for most of the year. The landscape is largely composed
of flat plains interspersed with sand dunes, reflecting the influence of wind erosion
and desertification (Zhang et al., 2020).

The Government of Nigeria recognises that achieving sustainable development
in the country depends on prioritising and effectively addressing poverty,
inequalities, insecurity, and climate change. In identifying adaptation priorities

     i.     Agriculture: About 10 to 25% decline in agricultural yield has been projected
            by 2080 because of climate crisis under Business-as-Usual scenario
            (FMEnv, 2021b).

     ii.    Water Resources: Nigeria is already experiencing rainfall variability across
            all the 4 major ecological zones. The southern states are having increasing
            rainfall intensity with attendant flooding, but the northern states are facing
            a decline in precipitation, causing more drought and decreasing surface
            water. Current reports show that Lake Chad has lost over 93 percent of its
            45,000 km2 area as at 1960 which is largely attributed to climate change.

     iii. Energy: Nigeria’s power sector is fragile and climate-sensitive, with grid
            collapses linked to both floods and extreme heat. Floods inflicted ₦329
            million in direct damage to power assets in 2012, while heatwaves caused
            two national grid collapses in one week as surging demand overloaded
            infrastructure in 2024 (CBA, 2025). Energy infrastructure remains
            concentrated in high-risk flood zones, further elevating baseline losses.
            Energy access is poor, with over 86 million people lacking electricity, and
            the situation is worse in rural areas, where only 26% have access.

The cost-benefit analysis (CBA) of the main adaptation options for the agriculture,
water resources, and energy sectors, based on a 35-year evaluation period and a
10% social discount rate, used net present value (NPV), benefit-cost ratio (BCR),
and internal rate of return (IRR) as key indicators and yielded highly favourable
economic outcomes (CBA, 2025). At the aggregate level, the portfolio of adaptation
options generates highly positive results. By 2050, the total capital costs amount
to ₦18.3 trillion (USD 12.4 billion), increasing to ₦26.5 trillion (USD 18.0 billion) by
2080. These are substantial investments, yet the present value of benefits far
exceeds the costs, with BCRs of 2.32 in 2050 and 2.41 in 2080, and Net Present
Values (NPVs) of ₦15.3-16.6 trillion (USD 10.4-11.3 billion). This means that for every
₦1 (or dollar) invested in adaptation across all sectors, Nigeria gains at least ₦2.3
(or dollars) in avoided damages, productivity gains, and resilience co-benefits. This
exceeds the standard threshold of 1, clearly confirming the economic viability of
the combined climate adaptation portfolio.

4.3    Nature-Based Solutions

Nigeria is adopting nature-based solutions (NbS) to address current and
anticipated impacts of climate change and to realise low-carbon development.
The approach was highlighted in both the NDC 2021 and the Climate Change
Act. Nigeria is endowed with a wide diversity of ecosystems – from rainforests
through dry savannahs to the dry Sahel, flat coastal zones, high-altitude plateaus,
montane forests, and useful freshwater wetlands, all under various climatic
conditions. Nigeria will use these natural ecosystems to significantly reduce the
impact of extreme climate events such as floods, catastrophic storms, and severe
droughts, and to offset vast amounts of the world’s CO2 emissions (Nzegbule and
Udoka, 2024). By implementing NbS actions, the country will address adaptation
challenges with multiple additional benefits across sectors at relatively low cost,
and, according to the estimate of Griscom et al. (2017), has the potential to meet
20% of its mitigation needs by 2050. Successful implementation of NbS actions
will require eliminating policy barriers, such as improper agenda-setting and poor

 strategic leadership, and improving coordination and long-term monitoring to tackle
challenges. Institutions such as the NCCC, River Basin Development Authorities,
the Great Green Wall Sahara Commission, and the National Parks Service will be
