5    Considerations of Guiding Principles (Best Practices) in Angola’s NAP
Implementation
This chapter outlines Angola’s approaches to consider the most vulnerable people, identified in the Key
Climate Risks, Vulnerabilities, and Adaptation Needs chapter in the implementation of Angola’s NAP. The
following groups of people are identified as most vulnerable and, on the frontline, facing climate change
impacts, increasing their vulnerability to climate change impacts and hazards in Angola: (i) women, mostly
pregnant women ; (ii) infants and children; (iii) youth; (iv) people with disabilities; (v) local communities; and
(vi) smallholder crop farmers and fisheries. Thus, the implementation of Angola needs to recognize these
groups, ensuring that the planning, implementation, and monitoring, evaluation, and learning of adaptation
consider the priorities of these groups. Specific approaches to increase recognition, participation, and
inclusivity for each group are proposed in the following sections.

5.1    Angola Gender-Responsive NAP Process

In general, gender dynamics shape who is most vulnerable to climate impacts, who has the resources for
adaptation, and who participates in key decision-making that influences vulnerability levels and capacity to
adapt to climate change. In Angola, as elsewhere, girls, boys, and women participate in highly climate-
sensitive sectors, making them more vulnerable. Girls, boys, and women in Angola often shoulder unpaid
care, livestock care, and water collection work.

They are key to local food systems, and may have less secure access to education, land, finance, and
information. Overlooking these gaps risks maladaptation and weaker outcomes. International guidance for
NAPs under the UNFCCC calls for gender-responsive planning—embedding analysis, participation,



                                                                                                               35
 budgeting, and monitoring— as it measurably improves effectiveness.20,21 Given Angola’s high climate
vulnerability and relatively low readiness, 22 integrating gender across adaptation priorities is both a legal and
practical imperative for resilience.

Limited access to education for girls, boys, and women significantly reduces their adaptive capacity, coupled
with limited access to means of production. Recent gender statistics point to the specific vulnerabilities of
girls and women in Angola. The adult female literacy rate in Angola is 53.4% for girls aged 15 and above
(IIMS 2023-2024), with a disproportionate difference across urban (67.1%) and rural (34.2 %) areas,23 which
constrains access to climate information and services, significantly limiting their adaptive capacity.
Adolescent fertility in Angola remains among the world’s highest at ~123 births per 1,000 girls aged 15—19
(IIMS 2023-2024),24 compounding health and economic risks in climate shocks. Many households rely on
women’s incomes and leadership: about 26% of households are female-headed (IIMS 2023-2024),25

Across the country, women carry the burden of unpaid domestic labor, including collecting water and fuel—
tasks that become more arduous and dangerous during droughts and extreme weather events. In rural
communities, where only a small fraction of households have access to clean cooking fuels or electricity,
these responsibilities expose women and girls to health risks and environmental hazards. The lack of
infrastructure and services compounds their vulnerability, especially during crises.

Despite Angola being a highly urbanized country with approximately a third of the country population living
in the capital city of Luanda, approximately 3.7 million women still live in rural areas, out of which the 78%
report that agriculture is their main source of livelihood and often in rainfed systems sensitive to drought.26,
27
   Recently, the strong impact of El Niño caused one of the worst droughts in over 40 years, leaving a large
portion of the population, especially in rural areas, without sufficient food and water. As such, there is
increasing exposure to the risk of gender-based violence for girls and women.28 Together with Angola’s
ND-GAIN profile, these figures underscore gendered climate risk.

Climate change also deepens existing inequalities in decision-making. While some progress has been made,
only a minority of women, particularly in rural areas, have autonomy over their health and reproductive
choices. This limited agency affects their ability to respond to climate-related challenges, access healthcare,
and participate in community-level adaptation efforts.

5.2 Consideration of Children in Angola’s NAP Implementation

Children in Angola are highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Extreme weather events destroy
schools and key transport infrastructure required for children to access schools. Extreme heat affects



                                                                                                                    37
 children’s ability to learn, and exposure to higher-than-average temperatures is associated with fewer years
of schooling (UNICEF, 2019).

According to the Children’s Climate Risk Index (UNICEF, 2021), Angola ranks 10th globally in terms of
"extremely high risk" for children. As children in Angola experience deprivation of several needs
simultaneously, they are more vulnerable to the impact of climate change. Angola’s Multidimensional
Poverty Index shows that approximately 74.4%29 children experience between three and seven deprivations
simultaneously, with poverty being far more widespread among children under the age of 10. These
conditions make children particularly susceptible to the health, nutrition, education, and livelihood impacts
of climate-related shocks.

Rising temperatures, erratic rainfall, and increasingly frequent droughts and floods have severely disrupted
agricultural productivity, leading to widespread food insecurity and malnutrition. Malnutrition impairs
physical growth and cognitive development, reducing school performance and future economic potential. In
rural areas, where families rely heavily on subsistence farming, children are often pulled out of school to
help with household survival tasks such as collecting water and firewood, further jeopardizing their
education and safety (Climate Landscape for Children, UNICEF, 2023).

The health impacts are equally alarming. Climate-sensitive diseases, such as malaria, cholera, and diarrhoea,
are on the rise, exacerbated by poor sanitation and contaminated water sources—conditions worsened by
flooding and drought. Children in rural and poor urban communities are disproportionately affected, with
limited access to healthcare and vaccinations. Moreover, indoor air pollution from biomass fuels used for
cooking and lighting contributes to respiratory illnesses, with children bearing the brunt due to prolonged
exposure. The psychological toll of environmental disasters—loss of homes, livelihoods, and loved ones—
adds another layer of trauma, especially for young children who lack the emotional tools to process such
upheaval. Addressing these multifaceted challenges requires a coordinated, child-centered climate response
that integrates health, education, energy, and social protection systems.

The Angola NAP implementation adopts a child-centered approach that protects children’s rights, prioritizes
their needs, and includes their meaningful participation in decision-making processes. The following
approaches will be implemented to increase the consideration of children in the NAP implementation for
Angola.

     ● Consideration of adaptation actions that invest in and enhance climate-resilient water, sanitation, and hygiene
       (WASH), health, education, child protection, and social protection systems services;
     ● Incorporate child-specific vulnerability and capacity analysis into national and local climate change assessments;
     ● Integration of children in the monitoring, evaluation, and learning system, including setting age-disaggregated
       indicators, child-centered targets, and budget tags.

Climate change significantly undermines educational access and outcomes for children and youth in Angola,
particularly in rural and drought-affected regions. The CLAC report (UNICEF Angola, 2023) highlights that
over 2.3 million children are out of school, with droughts and extreme weather events disrupting both
attendance and infrastructure. In farming households, climate-induced income shocks often force families

 Boys in rural areas are vulnerable because of their livestock farming responsibilities, as they continuously
travel longer distances to feed and water livestock (FAO, 2014). Thus, limiting education opportunities.
Moreover, 70% of children have had their education disrupted due to climate-related factors, such as school
closures, non-attendance, or inability to concentrate (Philipp, 2021). The lack of access to electricity in many
schools further compounds this issue, limiting the use of educational technologies and distance learning,
especially during emergencies. These challenges threaten to deepen existing inequalities and hinder the
long-term development potential of Angola’s youth.

The long-term successful implementation of adaptation in Angola will depend largely on building the
demographic dividend through skills, technical capacities, and values of its people, backed by effective
systems. Education is therefore crucial—from pre-primary to higher educational levels (Universities), as well
as training programs that build the technical skills needed for planning and implementation of climate
adaptation that prioritize sustainable development. The youth will be one of Angola’s most important assets
in the transition to a climate-resilient and socially inclusive future economy that integrates adaptation at all
levels of planning and implementation of development activities.

5.4 Considerations of Local Communities and other Vulnerable Groups in the
    Implementation of the Adaptation Plan in Angola

5.4.1 Considerations of People with Disabilities in the Implementation of the
       Adaptation Plan in Angola

Climate change in Angola poses heightened risks for people with disabilities, who often face compounded
vulnerabilities due to limited mobility, access to services, and social exclusion. The CLAC report (UNICEF
Angola, 2023) highlights that adaptation strategies must be inclusive, noting that public health actions
should prioritize vulnerable groups, such as children, the elderly, pregnant women, and people with
disabilities. These groups are especially at-risk during climate-related disasters, such as floods and droughts,
which can disrupt access to healthcare, sanitation, and safe shelter.

Moreover, the lack of inclusive infrastructure and emergency response systems means that people with
disabilities may be left behind during evacuations or unable to access critical services. Ensuring that climate
resilience planning includes disability-sensitive measures—such as accessible health units, inclusive
education, and targeted awareness campaigns—is essential for safeguarding their rights and well-being in
the face of escalating climate threats.

Angola’s NAP process should fully ensure consideration of people with disabilities (PWD) due to their high
vulnerability to climate change impacts in the country. The Angola NAP process recognizes the important
role of adaptation that considers the needs of PWD, including their role and full participation of PWD in
adaptation decision-making processes at all levels of decision-making. To achieve this, the NAP process for
Angola prioritizes the following.



                                                                                                             40
  ● All information, communication, and materials related to the NAP process must be provided in accessible formats
    that people with disabilities can understand;
 ● Inclusive Participation and Representation in all activities of the NAP process;
 ● Targeted strategies for PWD in the implementation of adaptation actions that consider the unique challenges and
    needs of PWD, in areas such as social protection, employment, and access to resources and services.


5.4.2 Inclusion of Traditional Local knowledge in NAP Implementation for Angola

The planning and implementation of adaptation, at all levels of government (national and local) and sectoral,
should consider the diversity of knowledge, including the equal consideration of traditional and local
knowledge and practices. Also, the implementation of adaptation should be informed and guided by
traditional and local knowledge systems.

Recognizing this, the implementation of the Angola NAP process must ensure that these groups are given
special consideration. The following approaches will be applied to increase the participation of local
communities in the planning and implementation of adaptation in Angola. To increase the consideration of
traditional and local knowledge in Angola’s NAP process, the following approaches will be applied:

 ● Offer training that bridges different knowledge systems, promoting mutual understanding and respect;
 ● Facilitate intercultural dialogue to enhance collaboration between scientific, traditional, and local knowledge
    holders
 ● Promote active participation of local communities through participatory approaches;
 ● Apply community-based adaptation and locally led adaptation as key entry points for implementing adaptation
   actions;
 ● Co-create adaptation solutions with local communities, incorporating their knowledge systems into decision-making
   processes;
 ● Establish deep, respectful, and equitable partnerships between local communities and adaptation actors;
 ● Consider traditional and local knowledge and practices at every stage of the NAP process—from initiation and data
   collection to implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and replanning;
 ● Acknowledge and strengthen local governance structures to support collective decision-making and ensure
   inclusive adaptation planning and implementation;
 ● Integrate traditional and local knowledge into the monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) system of the NAP
   process; and
 ● Develop and apply disaggregated indicators to track the progress of adaptation actions informed by or implemented
   by local communities.

This chapter presents an overview of Angola’s current climate change-related vulnerabilities and key risks,
as well as its projected future vulnerabilities, risks, and potential impacts and losses.

The chapter presents a summary of the data and information available on climate change risks in Angola
based on the evidence available to date. This preliminary assessment outlines Angola’s current

6.1 Current Situation: Angola’s Historical and Present Climate Trends


                                                                                                                 41
 This section provides a concise overview of Angola’s historical and current climate trends. For more detailed
information, see Angola’s Second National Communication to the UNFCCC. 31

Angola is a southern African country with 1,650 km of Atlantic maritime coastline and land border of 4.837
km, bordering the Republic of Congo, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Republic of Zambia, and
Namibia.

Angola has a semiarid, narrow coastal region with average annual rainfall of 600 mm, with higher rainfall in
the north and lower rainfall in the south. Its interior plateau is divided into three agro-ecological zones:

       ●    A warm and humid northern zone characterized by heavy rainfall exceeding 1,500 mm per year and
            consistently high average temperatures above 22°C;
       ●    A central zone with a tropical climate moderated by elevations ranging from 1,000 to 2,500 meters,
            receiving between 1,250 and 1,500 mm of rainfall annually and experiencing average temperatures
            of 18°C to 20°C;
       ●    A semi-arid southwestern zone near the Kalahari Desert, where tropical continental air masses and
            the Benguela Cold Current contribute to relatively low temperatures during the hot season. 32

Angola’s seasonal temperatures do not range widely between its two seasons: a cooler, drier season Cacimbo
(June-September) and the rainy season (October-May) which is warmer and more humid.

Angola has conducted several studies and assessments at the national and local33 levels to identify climate
impacts, risks, and vulnerabilities, which have been published in its Initial National Communication (2012) 34,
Second National Communication (2021) 35, Nationally Determined Contributions (2025) 36, and National
Strategy on Climate Change 2022-2035.37

Temperature Trends

Since 1951, Angola’s average annual temperature has risen by approximately 0.2°C per decade, amounting
to a total increase of 1.4°C since the mid-20th century. The country’s climate zones range from arid to
temperate to tropical. As part of the World Bank’s Angola Country Climate and Development Report (2022), a
climate assessment was carried out analyzing past climate trends and projecting future changes in
temperature and rainfall up to 2060. 38 The results confirm that Angola has been warming since the mid-

6.2 Future National Climate Projections

6.2.1 Temperature Projections

Temperatures in Angola are expected to continue rising, especially under a high-emissions scenario, while
future rainfall patterns remain highly uncertain. The World Bank41 assessed two climate scenarios: a
moderate emissions pathway (RCP4.5) and a high-emissions pathway (RCP8.5). Under both scenarios,
models indicate that average annual temperatures across most of Angola will be 1—1.5°C higher in the
2020—2040 period compared to the 1981—2010 baseline. By 2040—2060, under RCP4.5, most of the
country is expected to warm by 1.5—2°C. Under RCP8.5, temperatures are projected to rise by 2—2.5°C,
with some southern areas reaching increases of 2.5—3°C, excluding coastal regions.

These changes have major implications for water resources, drought intensity, and localized extreme heat.
Additional research referenced by the IPCC shows that even if global warming is limited to 1.5°C, individuals
born in Angola in 2020 will face 7—8 times more heatwaves over their lifetime compared to those born in
1960. Under current climate pledges, which imply around 2.4°C of global warming, that number could
exceed 10 times more.

Key Impacts at National Level Related to Climate Hazards

The National Climate Change Strategy 2022-203549 identifies risks and vulnerabilities associated with the
types of hazards summarized in the preceding section on Angola’s people, ecosystems, and economy.

Floods: Due to the abundance of natural resources, communities in In rural regions, often settle near

The 2015 El Niño event impacted at least 1.4 million people across seven provinces, with 78 percent located
in southern Angola’s Cunene, Huila, and Namibe regions. In urban centers such as Luanda, Benguela, and
Namibe, floods have caused extensive destruction of homes and businesses and long-term disruptions to
transportation—largely due to urban expansion into flood-prone zones.

6.4.2 Gender

Women, men, girls, boys, and gender-diverse groups experience the impacts of climate change differently
due to unequal access to resources, decision-making power, and livelihoods. In Angola, 82 percent of women
workers were concentrated in nonwage jobs as compared to 57 percent of male workers. Many women play
a role as both the earner and the caretaker of the family, forcing them into unstable jobs such as street
vendors.61 The lack of economic opportunities and social protections makes women more vulnerable when
facing climate hazards, disasters, and forced migration.

Gender inequality in Angola is also reflected by the prevalence of gender-based violence and limited access
to sexual reproductive health services. The fertility rate in Angola is estimated to be 5.12 births per woman,
and only 50% of births are attended by skilled health personnel. 62 32% of Angolan women are estimated to
have suffered physical violence since the age of 15.63

Climate-induced disasters such as infectious diseases have serious consequences on maternal-fetal and child
health and increase the risks of gender-based violence. 64 In this context, safeguarding maternal and
reproductive health, guaranteeing equitable access to health, strengthening the leadership of women and
men in community-based resource governance, and ensuring that women (who are often primary users and

 6.4.3 Urban Populations

Urban populations, especially the poorest households and those living on marginal land, are highly exposed
to several climate hazards. Moreover, their well-being and livelihoods depend on urban infrastructure,
supply chains, and public services that are at high risk from climate change impacts. Key climate
vulnerabilities include but are not restricted to: 1) urban flooding impacting housing and infrastructure; 2)
droughts impacting urban water supply; 3) heatwaves exacerbated by the urban heat island (UHI) effect,
increasing energy costs from air conditioning use and air pollution, as well as heat-related illness and
mortality; and 4) public health risks including rising incidence of diarrhoeal disease and malaria, already
amongst Angola’s leading causes of death.65 66

6.4.4 Persons with Disabilities

An estimated 2.5% of Angolans live with disabilities (56 percent were men and 44 percent were women). 67
Recognizing the heightened vulnerability that people living with disabilities face with regard to climate
change impacts,68 further study is needed to better understand these risks and vulnerabilities in Angola to
design appropriate adaptation measures.

6.4.5 Local communities

Angola’s local communities include the San, the Himba, and other groups, including the Kwisi, the Kwepe,
the Kuvale, and the Zemba. Local communities face distinct vulnerabilities to climate change due to their
vulnerability and the natural ecosystems for their livelihoods. Further study is needed to better understand
climate change risks and vulnerabilities facing local communities in Angola to design appropriate adaptation
measures.

6.5.1.        Agriculture

The agricultural sector relies heavily on the climate and is therefore highly susceptible to the impacts of
climate change70. At the same time, it plays a vital role in enhancing the population’s overall nutritional well-
being. In recent decades, extreme climate fluctuations have endangered rural food security, leading to
greater crop losses caused by severe weather events.

The extended drought periods, particularly affecting the southern regions, have led to reduced water
availability, severely impacting agriculture and livestock. Projected temperature increases are expected to
accelerate evaporation, resulting in lower soil moisture and decreased yields for certain crops. Consequently,

Direct economic losses in Angola’s agricultural sector due to climate change from droughts could increase

have been less severe in the past, but will likely range between USD45 million and USD100 million per year
in multiple provinces. Total economic losses due to drought are driven by losses in agricultural production
(comprising 75 percent of average annual loss).

Annually, over 35 percent of the country’s total crop area is exposed to drought, and only a fraction of the
country’s arable land is irrigated. Recent modelling presented on the World Bank Climate Knowledge Portal
shows all provinces are likely to see decreased early-season rainfall (September— November period) by the
2060s, and there is some likelihood that rainfall in March—May will also decrease. A shorter, more
concentrated rainy season would negatively affect the growth cycles of most crops. An increase in the
magnitude (high likelihood) and extent of droughts (medium likelihood) would likely have devastating
impacts on agriculture.

The most negatively impacted crops will be maize, beans, and groundnuts, all critical crops for food security
and nutrition in Angola. Cassava, millet, sorghum, and banana, which are more drought-tolerant crops, will
be less impacted, and more climate-resilient crops like cassava will largely see an increase in suitability,
especially in the central regions. Southern regions will generally become less suitable for crop production,
with Namibe, Bie, Bengo and Moxico most affected.

In Angola today, land tenure and land management, resource tenure, agricultural development, and the
integration of environmental sustainability are regulated and managed in a limited or inadequate way and
need to be implemented/executed. Resource rights are essential to the promotion of sustainable land and
resource management.

The fragile nature of soils and vegetation increases the risks of environmental degradation, due to population
pressure and/or poor management of natural resources, such as overgrazing, deforestation for firewood
production, and land clearing.

 6.5.1.        Fisheries

The main vulnerabilities of the fisheries and aquaculture sector stem from the availability and distribution of
key fishery resources, as well as limitations in technical and institutional capacity 72. These factors are
influenced by variations in temperature and wind patterns, rising sea levels, and declining freshwater levels
affecting inland fisheries and aquaculture.

In the southern provinces of Benguela and Namibe, the coastal ecosystem relies on upwelling, which sustains
a nutrient-rich marine environment. Alterations in wind patterns affect this process—a reduction in wind
intensity diminishes nutrient supply, leading to fewer available fish resources. Meanwhile, the provinces of
Luanda, Zaire, and Bengo may experience the effects of more frequent and intense hot coastal winds, which
significantly impact marine biodiversity and overall fishing productivity.

Climate change is expected to impact fisheries in Angola, although research is limited, and models present
significant levels of uncertainty73. The country’s coastal fisheries lie in a historically productive zone within
the Benguela Current Large Marine Ecosystem (BCLME), one of the most productive ecosystems in the
world. Angola’s National Development Plan 2018—2022 identifies fisheries and aquaculture as a sector to
grow, aiming to remobilize 10 ships and achieve an average production of 303,000 tonnes of fish through
industrial and semi-industrial fishing, 232,400 tonnes from artisanal fisheries, and 3,580 tonnes from
aquaculture.

However, the combined effects of climate change on factors such as water temperature, current and
nutrient circulation, and pH may substantially change the distribution and composition of fish stocks
throughout the country, especially when combined with anthropogenic stressors (e.g., overfishing, habitat
degradation). In a high GHG emission scenario (RCP8.5), Angola’s maximum catch potential (MCP) is
expected to decrease by 43.7 and 64.0 percent by 2050 and 2100, respectively.

elements, including coastal dynamics and their driving forces, as well as socio-environmental conflicts and
the impacts of human occupation and activities.

6.5.1.        Forestry, Ecosystems and Biodiversity Sector

Forests play a vital role in providing environmental goods and services, including rainfall regulation, soil fertility
maintenance, erosion control, water conservation, flood mitigation, food provision, climate regulation, recycling of
harmful gases, carbon sequestration for climate change mitigation, and the preservation of biodiversity 78. They also
serve as a key source of livelihood for much of Angola’s population, offering timber and non-timber forest products,
medicinal plants, household fuelwood, and habitats for wildlife and other forest species that support the country’s
tourism industry.

Approximately 38% of Angola’s population lives in rural areas, relying heavily on forest resources for subsistence
and income. According to the national energy matrix, wood and charcoal dominate energy consumption, accounting
for 56.8% of total energy use, compared to 41.7% for kerosene, 1.45% for electricity, and just 0.1% for natural gas.

However, forests face increasing threats from deforestation caused mainly by the conversion of forest land for
agriculture, infrastructure, and human settlements—activities responsible for around 80% of forest loss. Additional
pressures include biofuel production, fuelwood collection, mineral and timber extraction, climate change, and the
spread of pests and diseases.

Angola’s National biodiversity strategy and action plan, 2019—202579 highlights some risks related to biodiversity
loss and climate change in addition to anthropogenic factors, and sets out actions for conservation, preservation,
protection, and restoration of biodiversity in Angola.

6.5.1.        Human Health

The following excerpt from Angola’s Second National Communication 81 describes risks and vulnerabilities related to
the health sector:

“In terms of human health, climate change tends to lead to an increase in the number of deaths related to prolonged
periods of high temperatures, an increase in diseases transmitted by water, food or other vectors, and a worsening
of the health problems associated with air pollution.

Rising temperatures and wetter conditions can have an impact on human health through a change in the geographical
distribution of diseases. Vector-borne diseases are sensitive to climatic factors. The IPCC projects that a 5-8%
increase in arid and semi-arid lands in Africa could increase transmission and favor the expansion of the meningitis
area.

Dengue is transmitted by the bite of the contaminated female Aedes aegypti mosquito. The expansion of the urban
environment, with poor sanitary infrastructure, is conducive to increasing the density of the vector population. If
torrential rain and flooding are more frequent in the future, they may create more suitable conditions for Dengue
fever, although there are several other factors.

Malaria is an acute or chronic infectious disease caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted
by the bite of the Anopheles mosquito. The presence of the malaria mosquito depends on temperature, humidity,
water, and wind. There is a possibility that malaria could spread to areas of Africa where it is rare for climatic reasons.
Higher temperatures may extend the range and seasonality of disease transmission caused by a vector, especially
malaria.

Cholera is a disease caused by Vibrio cholerae, a bacterium that rapidly multiplies in the human intestine, producing
a potent toxin that causes intense diarrhea. It only affects humans, and its transmission is directly from fecal waste
from patients by oral ingestion, mainly in contaminated water.

The IPCC Fourth Report concluded with certainty that human health in Africa could be negatively affected by climate
change instability (IPCC, 2007). Changing temperature and rainfall patterns will alter the ecology of some disease
vectors, thus altering the manifestation of certain diseases. Much research in this field has focused on malaria, but
there are also risks of changes in the manifestation of dengue fever, meningitis and cholera. Some of the direct
effects of climate change on health are floods, droughts, and heat stress. Some of the indirect effects are the spread
and/or increase in the incidence of infectious and vector-borne diseases, water-borne pathogens, water and air
quality, and food availability and quality. The actual future impacts depend heavily on local environmental conditions,
the socio- economic situation of the area, and existing adaptation measures to reduce threats.

Vulnerability is the ability of a community or communities to adapt to health threats depending on their overall
health status. In this respect, factors such as the prevalence of cardiovascular disease, HIV and TB, malnutrition or
atrophy especially in children, level of education and awareness, economic status, general demographic profile,
migration patterns and levels, level of development and maintenance of infrastructure, access to and availability of
skilled medical personnel and facilities, and population density are considered.

Between 2008 and 2010, Angola was the target of storms resulting from rainfall changes that could reflect climate
change, with unusually heavy rains that motivated more than two hundred thousand environmental refugees and
seven dozen deaths in addition to the death of livestock and the loss of biodiversity due to the accumulation of
water resulting from abnormal rainfall. The consequences of the rains that fell in this period in the provinces of
Cunene and Cuando Cubango82 were also due to anarchic human settlements, poor water management, lack of
urban planning, and other factors, which characterize the state of vulnerability to which the populations are exposed.

The phenomenon of high urban temperatures is called the urban heat island. Urban heat islands cause discomfort in
cities with a tropical and warm climate. Changes in air humidity, rainfall, and wind are also associated with the
presence of urban heat islands. Heat islands aggravate heat waves (heat waves) with consequences such as sleep
disturbance or health impacts.

6.5.1.    Further sectors

In addition to the seven priority sectors of this NAP whose risks and vulnerabilities are described above, further
vulnerability analysis should be done for the energy and the education sectors.

    ●    Energy: Angola has one of the highest hydropower potentials in Africa, estimated at 18,200 MW, and
         hydropower has historically been the country’s primary source of electricity. By 2020, nearly 90 percent of
         Angola’s electricity was generated from hydropower, up from about 70 percent in 2019, with the remainder
         coming from oil products and gas. However, hydropower generation is highly dependent on upstream flow
         conditions, which are becoming increasingly unpredictable due to climate change.

    ●    Projections suggest that southern and southeastern Angola will experience drier conditions, potentially
         reducing hydropower output in rivers such as the Kunene, which borders Namibia. While some river basins
         may benefit from increased runoff, this could also lead to more intense precipitation events, resulting in
         flooding and accelerated soil erosion. Such erosion carries sediment into reservoirs, reducing their storage
         capacity and further limiting energy production. These changes may lead to a decline in annual hydropower
         output, possible increases in electricity costs, and amplified flood risks that could negatively impact
         communities, infrastructure, and agriculture.

    ●    Education. Acknowledging that children's education is disrupted by climate change, this is also a vital sector
         to build adaptive capacity of children and young people, with flow on benefits for their families and
         communities. Angola has adopted its National Education Plan (2017-2030), which can strengthen its
         integration of climate change considerations in Education, and future iterations of the NAP may engage
         Climate Education as a priority sector to address the human capital challenges and vulnerabilities of children
         and youth.

 8.5 Other Support Needs Required for Implementation of Angola NAP

In addition to the finance required to support the implementation of priority adaptation actions, technology and
capacity needs are critical. These are crucial for the effective implementation of the NAP process for Angola. This
section outlines the key technology and capacity needs required.

8.5.1.     Adaptation Technology Needs

Angola has not yet conducted a full technology needs assessment for adaptation, nor for mitigation, a gap identified
in the ENAC. Therefore, the NAP presents an opportunity for Angola to conduct a technology needs assessment
that can comprehensively assess the level of technology needs required to successfully implement adaptation in the
country. Thus, as part of the GCF Readiness Programme, a technology needs assessment for adaptation can be
commissioned. The technology needs were identified through stakeholder consultation and expert solicitation, as
well as from other key national documents, such as the NDC, ENAC, and Angola’s Second National Communication
(SNC) etc. Aligning with the Paris Agreement, article 10 requires that other technology needs be transferred from
different regions, from developed and developing regions through international cooperation. There is potential for
technology development and transfer for Angola’s NAP to utilize existing frameworks in the UNFCCC, including the
Technology Mechanism. The technology needs expressed in Table 15 are additional to the specific technologies
described in adaptation actions in Table 12. The list here is just the key needs and is not exhaustive.

8.7 Adaptation Finance Gap for Angola

Compared to the financial resources required to implement the Angola NAP , the available domestic public resources
and international finance received by Angola fall short of addressing the needs, indicating an adaptation finance gap.
Other key sectors prioritized in this NAP are yet to receive international funding for the implementation of
adaptation activities. This highlights the need to broaden the finance base by mobilizing resources from multiple and
diverse sources to close the adaptation finance gap. Thus, a pragmatic investment plan for the adaptation sector is
required, to address practical steps to close the adaptation finance gap.

8.8 Private Sector Participation in Financing the Angola NAP Implementation

The participation of the private sector in adaptation is critical for providing a broad base of adaptation investments
required to close adaptation finance gap identified in this NAP. To increase private sector investment in the
adaptation sector, Angola aims to implement the following measures:


                                                                                                                              112
 Improvements in standardized metrics for project impact: Angola will invest in improved adaptation costing. This
would allow the private sector to clearly estimate the investment costs required and assess the risk, which is critical
for building an investment case for adaptation projects in the country.

Provide adequate climate risk data: Angola will increase access to climate data and risk information and other
localized climate information in the country and ensure its public availability to assist the private sector make
informed decisions on adaptation investments. Increased access to reliable climate data and information helps the
private sector identify risks and opportunities, fostering confidence in adaptation investments. This is because data
and knowledge gaps make it difficult to identify, develop, and prepare potential climate adaptation projects for public
and private investors (OECD, 2023).

Create enabling policies in Angola: Angola will implement clear and supportive legislation, policies, and regulatory
frameworks, such as land-use policies and building codes that incentivize adaptation, allowing for sufficient
incentives for the private sector to invest in adaptation across the key sectors identified in this NAP. High investment
risk in developing countries limits investment attractiveness for private sector participation in adaptation (CPI, 2024).
With the establishment of correct and supportive policies in place, this has the potential to be reduced. To create an
enabling policy environment that will attract private sector investments in adaptation, Angola will implement the
following measures.

    (i) Invest in “last mile” solutions to expand access to climate data, such as online platforms;
    (ii) Integrate climate adaptation into project preparation facilities;
    (iii) Enhance coordination mechanisms through a country platform linked to national priorities.

Address high upfront costs required for adaptation: This can be achieved by offering blended finance, credit
enhancement, and other targeted risk reduction or revenue-boosting measures that are important for de-risking
mechanisms for the private sector in Angola. This can also be achieved through the implementation of financial
incentives, such as tax breaks and public funds that de-risk adaptation investments. Transaction costs can be high
relative to the size of the project, particularly where innovative technologies are being used, or the investment
involves multiple beneficiaries (OECD, 2024). Thus, government measures to address transactional costs will be
prioritized.

Foster public-private partnerships: Angola will implement blended finance mechanisms that combine public and
private capital and de-risking instruments to reduce investor concerns. The co-designing of solutions will be
prioritized to ensure alignment with national climate priorities and leverage public sector support.

Foster collaboration: By creating business sector panels and knowledge-sharing platforms in Angola, this offers the
learning opportunities required to attract more private sector participation in the adaptation sector.

Deploy public and blended finance instruments strategically to mobilize private finance for adaptation. There is a
need for international providers to better understand and link private investors’ preferences, notably for secure
revenue streams, with specific characteristics of adaptation projects. Measures for Angola here include scaling up
approaches, such as risk sharing, using intermediaries to address financiers' unfamiliarity with adaptation, and
revising mitigation-related bankable projects to heighten their contribution to adaptation.

8.10 Domestic Resource Mobilization for Adaptation

The ENAC 2022—2035 identifies funding sources available for climate adaptation from domestic public resources
in Angola. Although these available sources may offer low volumes compared to the required resources, they provide
important resources required to support adaptation by the country. The domestic public funding sources relevant
for the implementation of Angola’s NAP include the following.

National Environment Fund: The FNA was created in January 2011 and is administratively supervised by the
Ministerial Department responsible for the Environment. Its objectives are: (i) Financial support for environmental
management, promotion, and conservation; (ii) Contribute to the promotion of activities related to the rational
management of environmental protection areas, rehabilitation, or recovery of degraded areas; (iii) Support the
realization of technical-scientific activities for the introduction of clean technologies; (iv) Support civil society
activity. The FNA can provide resources for funding many adaptation actions across sectors in conservation,
particularly forestry, ecosystems, and biodiversity.

Angolan Agricultural Development Support Fund: Created under Executive Decree 40/87, FADA was reactivated
in October 2016 under the Ministry of Finance as a "specialized financial institution" to support the country's
agricultural development policy. The fund is intended to be an instrument for boosting agriculture, one of the priority
sectors for diversifying, the national economy. The government intends to develop the sector by promoting the local,
regional and national economy and by being a driving force for the fulfilment of SDG 2: Eradicate hunger, achieve
food security, improve nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture. This fund is important for supporting the
implementation of priority adaptation actions in the agriculture and food sector identified in this NAP.

Sovereign Fund of Angola: Established in 2008 to promote growth, prosperity, and socio-economic development in
Angola. In 2011, the Fund was legally ratified and officially established as Angola's Sovereign Wealth Fund, with an
initial endowment of 5 billion dollars. Its aim is to promote Angola's social and economic development by generating
wealth for the Angolan people. The fund is key for financing adaptation actions, such as expanding social protection
measures identified in Section 7. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning Framework for Angola NAP

9.2 Integration of the National Adaptation Plan in the National Development Plans

the national, sectoral, and local levels to achieve long-term development goals, addressing some of the barriers on

ensuring that adaptation in Angola strengthens existing development objectives, making them more resilient to
climate impacts, and aligning them with long-term national development strategies. A hybrid model of simultaneous
national and sector-specific consideration of adaptation integration in national development plans will be adopted.

The integration and mainstreaming of Angola’s NAP will take place at two levels.

●      Vertical integration at the national and local (provincial and local municipality) planning level Vertical integration allows the
       creation of strategic linkages between national and local governance levels for planning, implementation, and monitoring;

●      Horizontal integration at the sector or cross-sectoral planning level: Horizontal integration involves mainstreaming climate
       adaptation across key development sectors for Angola, including agriculture, fisheries, water, coastal zones, health,
       infrastructure, forestry, and ecosystem and biodiversity.

9.5 Implementing Follow-Through Process for Integrating Adaptation in Angola

To fully understand the integration of the NAP into centrall, local, and sector planning and development processes,
a follow-through approach will be adopted by the government of Angola. The follow-through process will be
supported by political will from the government. A follow-through process for Angola refers to the continuous and
iterative cycle of implementing, monitoring, evaluating, and learning from adaptation actions after the initial planning
phase. It involves integrating adaptation into broader policies, coordinating efforts across sectors, and facilitating
the reporting and updating of the plan based on lessons learned, ensuring that adaptation efforts are sustained,
updated, and effectively integrated into national development.

The follow-through will take place at two levels: (i) central, local and (ii) sectoral levels. A successful follow-through
process for Angola’s NAP ensures that the benefits of adaptation (reduced losses and damages, economic, social,
and environmental benefits) are integrated into national development processes, thus improving the welfare of the
people, achieving the goal of this NAP: “eradicating poverty and attaining sustainable development.”

are presented in the MEL Section. Here, national targets and indicators are measuring the progress of adaptation

10.2 Role of Non-state Actors in the Implementation of the NAP

Non-state actors (NSAs), including NGOs, businesses, communities, and local organizations, play a critical role in
implementing the Angola NAP. These stakeholders provide local knowledge, foster community engagement,
innovate solutions, and ensure that adaptation actions are tailored to specific contexts. These will act as crucial links
between the government and citizens, raising awareness, disseminating information, and providing valuable
feedback on policy implementation. The key roles of the NSA in the implementation of the NAP include the
following:

Facilitating Local Engagement and Ownership: Local organizations will help increase community participation and
ownership in adaptation processes related to this NAP, ensuring that a broader policy framework is aligned with
local needs and ambitions.

Bridging Information Gaps: They will serve as a vital link, communicating the NAP to the public and conveying
community feedback to policymakers.

Monitoring and Accountability: By participating in review processes and providing direct feedback, the NSAs will
help ensure that Angola’s NAP implementation is effectively conducted and hold key stakeholders accountable.

Supporting Vertical Integration: NSAs will play a key role in providing crucial local perspectives and on-the-ground
insights, supporting the vertical integration of the NAP from the central to the local level.


                                                                                                                               123
 To facilitate NSA participation in the implementation of the Angola NAP, the following approaches will be taken.

 ● Create an enabling environment through clear communication that ensures NSAs receive clear information on NAP progress,
    their specific roles, and how they can contribute to the strategy; foster dialogue and partnerships that encourage cooperative
    relationship between government and NSAs; and build the capacity of NSAs through training and technical assistance to
    build the necessary capacity and expertise of NSAs for their roles in the NAP implementation.



 ● Integrating NSAs into the NAP Implementation by involving them in all stages of planning, implementation, and monitoring
    of adaptation; developing a system for tracking adaptation funding and activities; and making information accessible to NSAs,
    fostering trust and ownership.


10.3 Role of International Organizations in the Implementation of the NAP

International organizations play a key role in delivering impactful projects required for the implementation of the
adaptation actions in this NAP, mostly the international organizations with country offices in Angola, as they are
involved in the day-to-day running of activities and projects that are key in achieving the adaptation actions. These
include the UNDP, UNICEF, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), World Food Programme
(WFP), Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and International Labor Organization (ILO).

Most of these organizations are accredited entities for the main climate funds: the GCF, GEF, Adaptation Fund, and
LFCD; hence, they are implementing partners for the majority of the funding accessed from the climate funds. Other
relevant international organizations with regional offices that cover operations in Angola include UNEP, UN-Habitat,
AfDB, Conservation International, World Bank, USAID etc. Most of these organizations are also accredited entities
of the main climate funds.

10.4 Converting Adaptation Actions into Fundable Adaptation Projects and Programs

This section outlines how adaptation actions listed in Section 7 are converted into fundable projects that can be

Hence, as part of the implementation strategy, this section provides a framework to achieve actions to fundable

11 Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning Framework for Angola NAP
A monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) framework is applied to assess, monitor, and evaluate the progress and
effectiveness of Angola NAP implementation. The monitoring, evaluation, and learning framework for this plan has
been broken into three components: (i) monitoring, (ii) evaluation, and (iii) learning, ensuring that each component of
the MEL framework receives equal attention. Monitoring will ensure that the level of implementation of the NAP is
understood and appreciated from daily activities and progress toward the outputs of the plan. The Evaluation
component will provide periodic and ongoing feedback to improve the implementation of the plan, ensuring the
assessment of the overall success, effectiveness, and long-term impact are understood.

The Learning component ensures that the data, knowledge and experience gathered from the implementation of
Angola NAP and its MEL framework are utilized by relevant stakeholders to make better decisions, including the

                                                                                                                             124
 development of the next NAP or related strategies, frameworks and policies. The MEL framework is strongly linked
to national implementation reports, including synergies on international reporting in Section 12.




Figure 9: Conceptual framing of the MEL system of Angola NAP.




To effectively implement the MEL framework presented in this plan, Angola must establish and operationalize a MEL
system immediately. To pilot the design of the MEL system, a diagnostic/situational analysis is critical and should be
conducted to understand the information available. This allows the MEL system to be built from existing systems
starting at the gaps. The diagnosis can start with key sectors, such as water, agriculture, fisheries, and coastal zones.
This will provide key information for designing and piloting the MEL system for Angola’s NAP. Given the urgency
and importance of the MEL system in the overall implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and reporting (Figure 11)
of the NAP, the establishment of the MEL system should start as early as possible in 2026, and this is recommended
to be part of the GCF NAP Readiness Programme activities.

11.1 Approaches for MEL

11.1.1. Monitoring

Monitoring in NAP implementation provides information to check if activities are being carried out as planned,
resources are being utilized effectively, and progress is being made toward stated goals (Beauchamp, et al., 2024).
As part of the NAP implementation, monitoring involves tracking progress on national adaptation, including the
implementation of NAP processes and the results. It helps to answer questions such as “Is the implementation of
NAP processes proceeding as intended?” (Beauchamp, et al., 2024).

 ● Monitoring the progress of the implementation of Angola NAP constitutes operationalizing the Plan. Progress of
    implementation will be assessed at four levels and are as follows.

 ● Assess the progress of integration of the NAP in central and local sectoral planning and development. This is the first level
   of understanding Angola’s adaptation implementation process. This monitors the level of integration and mainstreaming of
   the NAP in national, local, and sectoral planning. The successful integration of adaptation in planning and development
   processes is critical for effective implementation of the NAP and crucial for building the country’s long-term resilience to
   climate impacts.



                                                                                                                           125
  ● Assess the progress of implementation of adaptation actions by priority sector. This will monitor the progress of
   implementation of the adaptation actions prioritized in this NAP.

 ● Assess progress of international support needed and received (finance, technology, and capacity) or mobilized. This monitors
   the progress of international support received and mobilized (international and domestic) towards NAP implementation —
   integration of NAP into national planning processes and the implementation of the adaptation actions.

 ● Assess progress on communication, uptake, and assimilation of lessons learnt from NAP implementation: This monitors the
   progress of communicating and uptake of lessons learned from the implementation of NAP into relevant and key sectors’
   decision-making and for future national climate adaptation processes, such as future NAPs, NDCs, etc.

11.2 Evaluation of Progress of Implementation

The evaluation of the progress of implementation for the Angola NAP process assesses the overall success,
effectiveness, and long-term impact of the implementation of the plan through periodic, in-depth analysis to draw
conclusions and inform future decisions. The evaluation will use both data from the monitoring process and
 information from other sources to determine the performance or success of implementation of the Angola NAP
against the targets set for each sector.

The evaluation of the Angola NAP implementation will occur at three levels:

NAP project-level evaluation. This level evaluates the progress of achieving goals and objectives of specific activities
of the NAP, which will take place at the program or project level that are implemented as part of the NAP activities.
Thus, the completion of adaptation projects related to the NAP will have its own project-level evaluation. A database
that captures the details of every program or project-related evaluation will be created and maintained as a section
of the MEL system. These will provide key data for an in-depth comprehensive evaluation in the first approach. This
also provides data for international reporting in the BTRs.

Bi-annual evaluation: A national progress report will take place every two years, based on i) the assessment of the
monitoring data from indicators, ii) assessment of project level evaluations; and iii) other relevant sources such as
research and has synergies with biennial transparency reporting to UNFCCC by Angola. Thus, the bi-annual
evaluation will inform the bi-annual national report that forms the document that will be submitted by Angola as an
adaptation section in the BTR. Thus, the first report is expected to be produced in 2026. Regular progress reporting
helps improve the capacity of reporting entities, ensuring constant learning and feedback.

Comprehensive evaluation. At this level, the evaluation will take place every four years, aligning with the detailed
national progress reporting suggested in Section 13. Thus, the results of both monitoring and evaluation processes
will be reported in the national progress report (which will be commissioned every four years of the NAP period
(Figure 11). The comprehensive evaluation of the Angola NAP implementation will typically provide details on the
following questions.93

     ● How effective has the implementation of Angola’s NAP been to date?
     ● What could be improved for the remainder of the plan?
       a) Has adaptation occurred and how sustainable is it under future climate risk?
     ● Have the benefits of adaptation been equitably distributed across different genders and social groups?
     ● Will the resilience results be sustained?

The Angola detailed progress reports are critical for informing the GST process. The last comprehensive and detailed
progress report will take place in 2033, two years before the NAP ends. This provides Angola with important
information required to start planning NAP 2.0, which will be approved in 2035. Figure 11 illustrates the reporting
structure for Angola NAP (2025 – 2035) in relation to national and international reporting including other global
processes, such as the GST.

The feedback from the evaluation process will inform the mid-term review of the NAP in 2030, given that the first
evaluation will take place in 2029, that is, after the first four years of the NAP process. This ensures alignment with
the review of the NAP, which is due in 2030, as the results from the comprehensive and detailed report are crucial
inputs for the review process. This timeline also aligns with the broader GGA process, as the targets in the UAE
Framework for Global Climate Resilience will end in 2030. The comprehensive, detailed national reporting timeline

11.3 Learning

This section outlines how the lessons learned from Angola NAP implementation will help inform its future adaptation
planning processes. It also describes plans for learning and how experience from other regions would be integrated
into enhancing national adaptation practices.

Learning for MEL systems of NAP implementation refers to the collective and deliberate process of acquiring,
assessing, and disseminating new knowledge that results in changed or reinforced knowledge, attitudes, and
behaviors related to climate change adaptation (Beauchamp et a., 2024). This definition underscores that learning is
both a process and an outcome. The process of learning, through dedicated activities involving acquiring, assessing,
and sharing new knowledge, does not on its own constitute learning. The learning process from Angola NAP
implementation needs to lead, or contribute, to some form of outcome, such as a change in knowledge, attitudes, or
behaviors. The monitoring and evaluation process described in the sections above must be actively oriented to
support learning throughout the Angola NAP implementation. Following this approach, the monitoring process for
Angola NAP will provide a basis for learning by tracking how implementation of the NAP is progressing. The
evaluation process will support learning by considering the wider impacts of the implementation, and by
interrogating in detail how and why changes have occurred, what has and has not worked, for whom, and why. The
learning enables Angola NAP implementation to be adjusted to address gaps, inequities, and shortcomings, correct
actions.

Learning for the Angola NAP will address the following important questions.

  ● What lessons can be drawn to improve the management of NAP implementation to ensure that it delivers actions in a timely,
    coordinated, and efficient manner, and prevent maladaptation?
 ● Have we encountered success and failure from NAP implementation?
 ● How should we review and improve NAP implementation?

12 Reporting and Communicating NAP Implementation
Reporting progress on NAP implementation is crucial for promoting accountability, ensuring continuous
improvement, and communication with stakeholders, such as governments, citizens, and the international process.
Angola NAP reporting will be conducted at national reporting while creating synergies with international adaptation
reporting in the UNFCCC. This section outlines the approach to reporting NAP implementation for Angola.

The following highlights why it is important for Angola to report progress on NAP implementation.
 ● Accountability and Learning: The reporting of the NAP implementation provides evidence to answer key questions about
   adaptation efforts by Angola, such as "Are we on track?" and "Are our adaptation efforts working?" This facilitates adaptive
   management by allowing course correction and continuous learning.
 ● Strategic Improvement: By synthesizing information from MEL activities, the progress report offers actionable insights that
   drive improvement in both the Angola NAP process and the MEL system.
 ● Communication and Transparency: Progress report narrates Angola’s adaptation story, communicate achievements,
   challenges, and lessons learned to a broad range of stakeholders, including citizens, businesses, development partners, and
   the global community.
 ● Facilitating Adaptive Management: The process of Angola’s reporting of its NAP implementation supports a dynamic, "learn-
   by-doing" approach to adaptation, even before a fully developed MEL system is established.
 ● Global Assessment: Regular reporting helps assess the overall effectiveness of NAP processes in contributing to the Global
   Goal on Adaptation outlined in the Paris Agreement.
 ● Informing Future NAPs: Implementation reports provide valuable data and experience for developing the next versions of
   the NAP, ensuring that they remain relevant and effective over time.


12.1 National Reporting on Progress of NAP Implementation

Angola will conduct national-level progress reporting of its NAP implementation, communicating in detail the
progress to its stakeholders and citizens. National reporting will communicate in detail the progress of NAP
implementation to relevant stakeholders. The national reporting of NAP implementation for Angola will serve as a
"health check-up", providing evidence of what is working and what is not, thereby enabling adaptive management
and strategic reflection to enhance future adaptation planning and implementation. Figure 9 illustrates the iterative
process for Angola conducting national reporting for the NAP. The national monitoring indicators in Section 11 form
the basis in which progress monitoring will be conducted. The progress report will also inform the three main reports
to communicate Angola’s progress of adaptation implementation to the international process, creating synergies
with international processes.

12.2 Synergies with Reporting on Adaptation Internationally

Angola’s reporting and communicating of progress on adaptation to the international process demonstrates good
practices that enhance transparency. Angola’s reporting of progress to the international community not only
communicate and showcase the progress of NAP implementation but also allows the sharing of experience and the
lessons learned with other LDC countries. It additionally contributes to the evidence for assessing the collective
progress on achieving the Global Goal on Adaptation, in alignment with the UAE Framework for Global Climate
Resilience.

 As described in the previous section, to allow synergies with GGA reporting, national reporting is proposed to be
conducted in 2029 and follow the GGA themes in the USE Framework for Global Climate Resilience. With the first
comprehensive and detailed reporting set to be conducted in 2029 and some of the GGA targets in the UAE
Framework for Global Climate Resilience coming to an end the following year, ensuring that information from NAP
implementation reports feeds into the country status report of achieving the GGA. Thus, national reporting for
Angola will provide granular, country-specific data needed to track and achieve the broader GGA objective.

Alignment at the indicator level: The progress of achieving the GGA will be assessed using 100 global indicators.
Details of how the data will be collected are not yet clear, but parties are most likely going to report the progress
through the three main vehicles described above: (i) BTRs, (ii) Adaptation Communications, and (iii) national
communications. However, it is important to create synergies between the reporting of GGA indicators and Angola’s
national indicators in Section 12. This ensures that the NAP report for Angola provides the relevant information
required for the synthesis of GGA indicators. To take advantage of the synergies, the indicators in the MEL section,
particularly priority sectors, are developed to allow issues from the national level to be aggregated in the synthesis
of information on GGA indicators.

The progress of implementation of adaptation for Angola is being reported and communicated to the international
process through:

 ● Biennial Transparency Reports
 ● Adaptation Communication Reports
 ● National Communication Reports

12.2.1.   Biennial Transparency Reporting

The Biennial Transparency Reporting (BTR) under the enhanced transparency framework is one of the established
channels in the Paris Agreement where progress on adaptation implementation is reported to the UNFCCC by
parties. For Angola NAP implementation, the BTR includes information on the implementation of priority adaptation
actions, levels of financial, technology development and capacity building needed and received. Therefore, in the
next cycle of BTRs (BTR 2 in 2026) and until 2035 when this NAP ends, it is important for Angola to include an
Adaptation Section, detailing how NAP implementation has progressed. To address the reporting burden for Angola,
the intermediary national report will constitute the Adaptation and Support Needs Received sections in the BTRs.

Although it is not mandatory for Angola to report on adaptation in the BTRs, doing so is important for showing
transparency with the international community on how Angola is advancing the implementation of adaptation that
protects its people, economy, and ecosystems. In this process, Angola can communicate progress and the gaps in
the support received for adaptation.

12.2.1.   Adaptation Communications

Adaptation communications (AdComs), established by Article 7, paragraphs 10 and 11 of the Paris Agreement, is
another channel through which Angola can report adaptation progress to the international process. In the AdComms,
Angola can include information related to its adaptation priorities in the NAP, the support needs received from
international community. Angola submitted its first AdComm in 2021 (in conjunction with the adaptation section in
NDC 2.0), which means that another one is due in 2025. Angola also submitted Adaptation Communication in

                                                                                                                 151
 conjunction with the adaptation section in NDC 3.0 in September 2025. However, this NAP replaces the Adaptation
Communication in NDC 3.0 and serves as the latest Adaptation Communication for the Republic of Angola. The next
Adaptation Communication will be submitted in 2029, communicating Angola’s progress of the implementation of
the NAP. To avoid reporting burden for Angola, the comprehensive, detailed national report will be submitted as the
AdComs. Applying decision 9/CMA.1 that guides the development of AdComs.

12.2.1.   National Communications

National Communications are progress reports submitted by Parties to the UNFCCC to inform the international
community about their activities and contributions to addressing climate change. Although not mandatory for Angola
— as an LDC country to submit its national communication, submitting it provides another opportunity for Angola
to report progress of NAP implementation, including gaps and challenges identified in the implementation of the
NAP and the support they need from the international community to achieve significant implementation that
addresses the gaps. Angola submitted its second national communication in 2021. In its next third national
communication, Angola could report progress of the implementation of this NAP.

12.3 Synergies with GGA reporting

As described in the previous section, to allow synergies with GGA reporting, national progress reporting is proposed
to be conducted in 2029, every 4th year after the adoption of the NAP. The GGA targets in the UAE Framework for
Global Climate Resilience will come to an end the following year, ensuring that information from progress reports
feeds into the country's status report of achieving the GGA. Thus, national reporting for Angola will provide granular,
country-specific data needed to track and achieve the broader GGA objective.

Alignment at the indicator level: The progress of achieving the GGA will be assessed using 100 global indicators.
Details of how the data will be collected are not yet clear, but parties are most likely going to report the progress
through the three main vehicles described above: (i) BTRs, (ii) Adaptation Communications, and (iii) national
communications. However, it is important to create synergies between the reporting of GGA indicators and Angola’s
national indicators in the MEL section. This ensures that the NAP report for Angola provides the relevant information
required for the synthesis of GGA indicators. To take advantage of the synergies, the indicators in the MEL section,
particularly priority sectors, are developed to allow issues from the national level to be aggregated in the synthesis
of information on GGA indicators. The diagnostic analysis conducted to initiate the development of the national MEL
system for the NAP will take stock of existing indicators, and ensure alignment in indicators and transparency
processes are maximized.
